families.stem: Write the following in interval notation: $\{{=v}:{=v}\in\mathbb{R},{=a}{=ls}{=v}{=hs}{=b}\}$
solution: The set holds every real number ${=v}$ from ${=a}$ up to ${=b}$, so the interval has the two ends ${=a}$ and ${=b}$, and the smaller number goes first.
At the left end the sign is ${=ls}$, so ${=a}$ {=lin} the set. This end therefore takes a {=lbn} bracket, ${=lb}$.
At the right end the sign is ${=hs}$, so ${=b}$ {=hin} the set. This end therefore takes a {=hbn} bracket, ${=rb}$.
Put the two ends together, separated by a comma: ${=lb}{=a}, {=b}{=rb}$.
families.notes: Standard: set notation to interval notation, both ends finite, all four bracket patterns (the book's ex6-1-2b shape with the ends and brackets varied). Marker uses the documented interval(lo, hi, closed_lo, closed_hi) with 1 = square bracket and 0 = round bracket; if the engine wants true/false for the two flags, change the two flag holes only. Computed strings use the Unicode sign <= (U+2264) rather than a LaTeX command so no backslash sits inside an expression string literal; check that the renderer shows it inside $...$. Answer key printed by the engine will be the interval notation, which is what the stem asks for. Unbounded ends are not used here because the plain marker syntax for infinity is not given; they are covered by the mcq family on infinite ends.

families.stem: Which of the following is the set notation for the interval ${=lb}{=a}, {=b}{=rb}$?
solution: The interval ${=lb}{=a}, {=b}{=rb}$ runs from ${=a}$ to ${=b}$, so the inequality has ${=a}$ on the left, $x$ in the middle and ${=b}$ on the right.
At ${=a}$ the bracket is {=lbn}, so ${=a}$ {=lin} the set and the sign is ${=ls}$.
At ${=b}$ the bracket is {=hbn}, so ${=b}$ {=hin} the set and the sign is ${=hs}$.
The set is $\{x:x\in\mathbb{R},{=a}{=ls}x{=hs}{=b}\}$.
families.notes: Standard: interval notation to set notation, both ends finite, all four bracket patterns (ex6-1-1b shape). mcq is natural here because each distractor is one specific bracket/sign mix-up: both signs flipped, only the left sign flipped, only the right sign flipped, so the four options are always distinct. The stem carries {=...} holes, so distinct_by_choices is not set. Computed strings use Unicode <= and < (no backslash in expression strings).

families.stem: Exactly one of the following sets can be written in interval notation. Which one?
solution: Interval notation such as ${=lb}{=a}, {=b}{=rb}$ stands for every real number between its two ends, with none left out.

A set over $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{N}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$ holds only some of the numbers between ${=a}$ and ${=b}$ (the integers, the counting numbers or the rational numbers), so it cannot be written as an interval.
Only the set over $\mathbb{R}$ holds all the numbers between ${=a}$ and ${=b}$, so it is the one that can be written in interval notation, as ${=lb}{=a}, {=b}{=rb}$.
families.notes: Advanced: classification twist. All four options share the same inequality; only the number system differs, so the one thing being tested is that an interval means every real number between the ends. Ends are positive (a from 1) so the set over N is never an empty or odd case, and b - a >= 3 keeps each non-real set non-empty. The stem is the same every time, so distinct_by_choices is true; a, d and the two signs give hundreds of different option sets. Uses the catalogued non-real-set misconception on all three distractors.

families.stem: Which of the following is the interval notation for the set $\{x:x\in\mathbb{R},x{=sg}{=c}\}$?
solution: The set holds every real number that is {=dirw}{=eqw} ${=c}$, so it runs on without end {=way}. One end of the interval is therefore ${=infw}$.
Infinity is not a number and can never be reached or included, so the bracket next to it is always round.
The sign ${=sg}$ at ${=c}$ means ${=c}$ {=cin} the set, so the bracket next to ${=c}$ is {=cbn}.
Write the end on the left first: ${=lbc}{=loc}, {=hic}{=rbc}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Square bracket written next to infinity
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student treats infinity like an end number that can be included, so writes a square bracket next to it, as in $[-\infty, 5]$ or $[5, \infty]$. Infinity is not a number and always takes a round bracket.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Half-line written running the wrong way
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student writes the interval that starts at the end number and runs the opposite way along the number line, for example $[5, \infty)$ for $x \le 5$ or $(-\infty, 5]$ for $x \ge 5$, matching the bracket to the sign but mixing up which side of the number the set lies on.

families.notes: Advanced: the twist the book itself uses, one end at infinity (ex6-1-1a/c/f, ex6-1-2a). The side param picks x less than c or x greater than c. Three single-error distractors, always distinct from the correct option and from each other: the finite end's bracket flipped (existing id), a square bracket at infinity (proposed), the half-line reversed with the finite bracket kept (proposed). Unicode infinity and sign characters are used inside computed strings so no backslash sits in an expression string literal; please confirm the renderer shows them inside $...$. Option pieces are mixed string/number lists indexed by side; if the engine rejects mixed lists, the fix is mechanical.

families.stem: To draw the graph of $y = {=a}x {=sg} {=abs(b)}$, a table of values is needed. Complete the table below by finding the $y$-value for each $x$-value. $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|}\hline x&{=x0}&{=x0 + 1}&{=x0 + 2}&{=x0 + 3}&{=x0 + 4}\\\hline y&?&?&?&?&?\\\hline\end{array}\end{aligned}$ Write down the five $y$-values, from left to right, separated by commas.
solution: Substitute each $x$-value of the table into the function $y = {=a}x {=sg} {=abs(b)}$ to find its $y$-value.

The completed table is $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|}\hline x&{=x0}&{=x0 + 1}&{=x0 + 2}&{=x0 + 3}&{=x0 + 4}\\\hline y&{=ys[0]}&{=ys[1]}&{=ys[2]}&{=ys[3]}&{=ys[4]}\\\hline\end{array}\end{aligned}$
The $y$-values, from left to right, are ${=ys[0]}, {=ys[1]}, {=ys[2]}, {=ys[3]}, {=ys[4]}$.
families.notes: Function to table: the 'create a table of values from a function in order to plot its graph' part of the objective. Same table layout as the book's Exercise 6-8 (the book leaves the cells blank; here they carry a ? so that a reader, and a blind solver, cannot misalign them). Standard because the function has both a coefficient and a constant, the coefficient is sometimes negative, and the x-values include negatives (a negative coefficient times a negative x is the sign step where students slip). The five y-values are asked as a list so every cell of the table is checked; the five points are the ordered pairs to be plotted. Instance ranges: |y| <= 19.

families.stem: The table below belongs to a linear function of the form $y = mx + c$. The cells marked ? are missing. Complete the table and identify the function. $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|}\hline x&{=xr[0]}&{=xr[1]}&{=xr[2]}&{=xr[3]}\\\hline y&{=yr[0]}&{=yr[1]}&{=yr[2]}&{=yr[3]}\\\hline\end{array}\end{aligned}$ Write down the equation of the function.
solution: The columns with $x = {=xs[0]}$ and $x = {=xs[3]}$ are complete, so the points $({=xs[0]}, {=ys[0]})$ and $({=xs[3]}, {=ys[3]})$ are both on the function.
From the first complete column to the second, $x$ goes up by ${=3 * d}$ and $y$ changes from ${=ys[0]}$ to ${=ys[3]}$, a change of ${=ys[3] - ys[0]}$.

For a linear function $y$ changes by the same amount for every step of 1 in $x$, so the number multiplying $x$ is ${=ys[3] - ys[0]} \div {=3 * d} = {=m}$. (Neighbouring columns are ${=d}$ apart in $x$, so $y$ changes by ${=m * d}$ from one column to the next, not by ${=m}$.)
Write $y = {=m}x + c$ and substitute the point $({=xs[0]}, {=ys[0]})$: ${=ys[0]} = {=m}({=xs[0]}) + c$, so $c = {=ys[0]} - ({=m * xs[0]}) = {=c}$.
The $x$-values go up by ${=d}$ each time, so the missing $x$-value is ${=xs[h]}$.
The missing $y$-value comes from the rule: for $x = {=xs[3 - h]}$, $y = {=m}({=xs[3 - h]}) {=sg} {=abs(c)} = {=ys[3 - h]}$.
The completed table is $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|}\hline x&{=xs[0]}&{=xs[1]}&{=xs[2]}&{=xs[3]}\\\hline y&{=ys[0]}&{=ys[1]}&{=ys[2]}&{=ys[3]}\\\hline\end{array}\end{aligned}$
The function is $y = {=m}x {=sg} {=abs(c)}$.
families.notes: Table to function, the book's 'complete the table and identify the function' (Exercise 6-8) with the twist that raises it to advanced: the x-values go up in steps of 2, 3 or 4 instead of 1, one x-value and one y-value are missing (in neighbouring middle columns, never in the two end columns, so two complete columns always pin the line down), and the function has both a coefficient and a constant. The trap the instance sets is reading the change between neighbouring y-values (m*d) as the coefficient of x when the x-step is not 1; the solution says so. Missing cells carry a ? rather than the book's blank so a reader cannot misalign them. The stem states the function is linear (y = mx + c), otherwise two points do not fix a function. c is never 0 so the sign word is always + or -. Instance ranges: x between -8 and 11, |y| <= 51.

params.require: L != T and L != T + 2 and T != L + 2

families.stem: A ball is released at the top of a ${=L}$ m slope and rolls to the bottom. The graph of $s(t)$ shows the distance, in metres, that the ball still has to roll, $t$ seconds after it is released. The graph is a straight line segment that starts at the point $(0, {=L})$ and ends at the point $({=T}, 0)$. The $t$-axis is drawn up to ${=A}$ and the $s$-axis is drawn up to ${=B}$. Which one of the following gives the domain of the function and what it represents?

choices.correct: $0 \le t \le {=T}$ s: the total time the ball takes to reach the bottom of the slope

distractors.text: $0 \le s \le {=L}$ m: the total distance the ball rolls down the slope
$0 \le t \le {=A}$ s: the total time the ball takes to reach the bottom of the slope
$0 \le t \le {=T}$ s: the distance the ball still has to roll

solution: The domain is the set of input values of the function. Here the input is the time $t$, so we read the domain from the horizontal axis.

The graph starts at $t = 0$, the moment the ball is released, and ends at $t = {=T}$, where $s = 0$ and the ball is at the bottom of the slope. The $t$-axis is drawn up to ${=A}$, but the graph does not go that far.
So the domain is $0 \le t \le {=T}$ s. It represents the total time the ball takes to reach the bottom of the slope.
The values $0 \le s \le {=L}$ m make up the range of the function, not the domain: they are the distances the ball still has to roll.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Reads the domain from the vertical axis
proposed_misconceptions.description: The learner gives the interval of the function values (the vertical axis) when asked for the domain, and so describes it as a distance instead of a time; domain and range are swapped.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the drawn length of the axis as the domain or range
proposed_misconceptions.description: The learner reads the domain from how far the axis is drawn instead of from where the graph starts and stops, so gives an interval that is longer than the graph.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Right interval, meaning taken from the other variable
proposed_misconceptions.description: The learner finds the correct interval of input values but says it represents the quantity on the other axis (the distance still to roll) instead of the time taken.

families.context: A ball is released at the top of a slope and rolls to the bottom. The graph of s(t) shows the distance, in metres, that the ball still has to roll, t seconds after it is released. The graph is a straight line from (0, L) to (T, 0).
families.stem: A ball is released at the top of a ${=L}$ m slope and rolls to the bottom. The graph of $s(t)$ shows the distance, in metres, that the ball still has to roll, $t$ seconds after it is released. The graph is a straight line that starts at the point $(0, {=L})$ and ends at the point $({=T}, 0)$. After how many seconds has the ball rolled ${=r}$ m?
solution: The graph shows the distance still to roll, not the distance already rolled. When the ball has rolled ${=r}$ m it still has ${=L} - {=r} = {=rem}$ m to roll, so we need the time $t$ at which $s(t) = {=rem}$.
The line goes from $(0, {=L})$ to $({=T}, 0)$, so the ball covers ${=L}$ m in ${=T}$ s, which is ${=q}$ s for every metre it rolls.
The ball has rolled ${=r}$ m, so $t = {=r} \times {=q} = {=ans}$ s. Check: the point $({=ans}, {=rem})$ is on the line, because the ball then still has ${=rem}$ m to roll.
families.notes: Reads the book's ball graph (ex6-1-8a) in the opposite direction: given an output-side fact, find the time. The twist is that s(t) is the distance still to roll but the question asks about the distance already rolled; a learner who reads s(t) = r gets q*(L - r) instead of q*r. The graph is described in words because the engine has no figure support (book figure checked: straight line (0, 10) to (20, 0), i.e. q = 2 for L = 10). Every instance has T = L*q, so the rate is a whole number of seconds per metre and every answer is a whole number; r runs from 2 to L-2, so the ball is neither at the start nor at the bottom. 108 instances.

families.context: A car travels along a straight road. The graph of s(t) shows the distance, in km, that the car has travelled t minutes after it set off. The graph is a straight line from the origin to a closed dot at the point (T, D), where the journey ends.

params.why: the car is still driving after h hours, so the time is inside the domain and some of the journey is left
the total distance D = v*T/60 is a whole number of kilometres

families.stem: The graph of $s(t)$ shows the distance, in $\text{km}$, that a car has travelled $t$ minutes after it set off. The graph is a straight line that starts at the origin and ends at a closed dot at the point $({=T}, {=D})$. How many kilometres of the journey does the car still have to travel after {=h} {=hword}?
solution: The closed dot shows where the journey ends. The domain is $0 \le t \le {=T}$ minutes and the range is $0 \le s \le {=D}$ km, so the whole journey is ${=D}$ km.
The time $t$ is measured in minutes, so {=h} {=hword} is $t = {=t0}$ minutes. This is inside the domain.
The graph is a straight line from the origin, so the distance travelled is proportional to the time: $s({=t0}) = \frac{{=D}}{{=T}} \times {=t0} = {=sv}$ km.
The distance still to travel is the whole journey minus the distance already travelled: ${=D} - {=sv} = {=ans}$ km.
families.notes: Builds on the book's car graph (ex6-8-11a: 'What distance did the car travel in an hour?' with t in minutes, the line from the origin to the closed dot at (120, 100)). It chains the book's own unit twist (an hour is t = 60) with what the range represents (the total distance is the top of the range) and a subtraction. The graph is described in words because the engine has no figure support; the straight-line reading is done by proportion, which is what a student reads off the gridlines in the book's figure (s(60) = 50). D = v*T/60 so the speed is a whole number of km/h and s(60h) = v*h is always a whole number; remaining distance is always positive. 36 instances.

families.stem: A hiker leaves a camp and walks along a trail. The graph of $h(t)$ shows the hiker's height, in metres above sea level, $t$ hours after leaving the camp. The graph is made of straight line segments that join the points $(0, {=h0})$, $({=t1}, {=h1})$, $({=t2}, {=h2})$ and $({=t3}, {=h3})$ in that order. Write the range of the function as an inequality in $h$, leaving out the units.
solution: The range is the set of output values of the function, here the heights $h$ that the graph reaches, so we read it from the vertical axis.
The graph passes through the heights ${=h0}$, ${=h1}$, ${=h2}$ and ${=h3}$ m. Between these points it is made of straight line segments, so it never goes higher or lower than one of these points.
The lowest point is ${=h1}$ m (at $t = {=t1}$) and the highest point is ${=h2}$ m (at $t = {=t2}$).
The range is not simply from the starting height (${=h0}$ m) to the finishing height (${=h3}$ m), because the graph goes below both of them and above both of them.
So the range is ${=h1} \le h \le {=h2}$.
families.notes: Range of a graph that falls, rises and falls again, so the range runs from the lowest to the highest point and not from the first to the last height (the book's range questions ex6-8-11c and ex6-1-8b read the range off a monotone graph, where first-to-last happens to be right; this is the twist). The graph is given as the four vertices of a polyline because the engine has no figure support. h0, d1, d2 and h3 are multiples of 50, with h1 < h3 < h2 and h3 != h0 enforced both in the drawing of h3 and in the constraints, so the minimum and maximum are always the two inner vertices, the answer differs from first-to-last in every instance, and h1 > 0. The marker writes both closed flags of interval(...) as 1 (both end points included, as the book's 0 <= s <= 100 does); check that the engine reads 1 as closed. At least 270 distinct height sets, times 8 time sets.

families.stem: The straight line ${=a}x + {=b}y = {=c}$ is to be sketched using the dual intercept method. Which one of the following correctly gives the $x$-intercept, the $y$-intercept and whether the graph is increasing or decreasing?
solution: Find the $y$-intercept by letting $x=0$: ${=b}y = {=c}$, so $y = {=Y}$. The $y$-intercept is ${=Y}$.
Find the $x$-intercept by letting $y=0$: ${=a}x = {=c}$, so $x = {=X}$. The $x$-intercept is ${=X}$.

To decide whether the graph is increasing or decreasing, write the equation in the form $y=mx+c$. Move the $x$-term to the other side of the equals sign (it changes sign) and divide every term by ${=b}$. This gives $m = {=m}$ and $c = {=Y}$, which agrees with the $y$-intercept found above.
The gradient $m = {=m}$ is {=msign}, so the graph is {=trend}. The sign in front of $x$ in the given equation is not the sign of $m$, because the $x$-term had to change sides.
The line passes through $({=X}, 0)$ and $(0, {=Y})$, so plot those two points and join them. Answer: $x$-intercept $= {=X}$, $y$-intercept $= {=Y}$; the graph is {=trend}.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the number on the right of the equation as the $y$-intercept
proposed_misconceptions.description: Treats the constant in $ax+by=c$ as the $y$-intercept, as it would be in $y=mx+c$, instead of letting $x=0$ and solving $by=c$, so the division by the coefficient of $y$ is skipped.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Changes the sign of an intercept when solving for it
proposed_misconceptions.description: After letting one variable be zero, treats dividing by the coefficient like moving a term across the equals sign and changes the sign of the answer, for example $3x=12$ giving $x=-4$.

families.notes: Advanced twist the book's two misconceptions point at: the equation is given as ax + by = c, not as y = mx + c, so the direction can only be read after rearranging. b is always positive, so the sign in front of x in the given equation is always the OPPOSITE of the sign of m; that is what makes the direction distractor a live error in every instance (it is exactly what a learner who reads the sign beside x as written would choose). Hand-checked: a=3, b=2, c=12 gives X=4, Y=6, m=-3/2, decreasing; a=-4, b=6, c=-12 gives X=3, Y=-2, m=2/3, increasing (checks: -4(3)+6(0)=-12 and -4(0)+6(-2)=-12). c = lcm(|a|, b)*k makes both intercepts whole numbers. Requires keep all five options distinct: X != Y (swap option), X != -Y (sign-flip option vs swap option); c is never equal to Y because b >= 2 and Y != 0. mcq is natural here: the answer joins two numbers with a classification (increasing or decreasing), and every distractor is one named, single error. Two new misconceptions are declared; the other two ids are from the catalogue. Uses only: let x = 0, let y = 0, then y = mx + c for direction, all the book's own method. Stem has holes, so distinct_by_choices is not needed.

params.why: otherwise the two intercepts are the same number and the order asked for in the stem would not matter
at least one intercept is a fraction, which is the twist the book uses in exercise 6.8 question 4a

families.stem: Determine the $x$-intercept and the $y$-intercept of the line ${=a}x - {=b}y = {=c}$. Give each intercept as a whole number or as a fraction in simplest form, and write the $x$-intercept first.
solution: To find the $y$-intercept, let $x=0$: $-{=b}y = {=c}$.
Divide both sides by $-{=b}$: $y = {=Y}$. The $y$-intercept is ${=Y}$.
To find the $x$-intercept, let $y=0$: ${=a}x = {=c}$.
Divide both sides by ${=a}$: $x = {=X}$. The $x$-intercept is ${=X}$.

Multiply both sides by $x$ (the equation is undefined for $x=0$, so $x\neq 0$): $0={=pa}{=aabs}{=pq}{=qx}x$.
Move the constant term to the other side: ${=qc}x={=na}$.
Divide both sides by ${=q}$: $x=\frac{{=na}}{{=q}}={=x0}$, so the $x$-intercept is $\left({=x0}, 0\right)$.
Domain: the denominator cannot be $0$, so $x$ can be any real number except $0$: $\{x: x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\neq 0\}$.
Range: the fraction ${=pa}\frac{{=aabs}}{x}$ can never equal $0$, so $y$ can never equal ${=q}$: $\{y: y\in\mathbb{R},\ y\neq {=q}\}$.
So the $x$-coordinate of the $x$-intercept is ${=x0}$, $x$ can never be $0$, and $y$ can never be ${=q}$.

families.stem: A student is asked to sketch the hyperbola $xy = {=a} {=sg} {=abs(q)}x$. Which description of the sketch is correct?

choices.correct: The branches lie in the {=br} regions formed by the asymptotes; the asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = {=q}$; the $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$.

distractors.text: The branches lie in the {=br} regions formed by the asymptotes; the asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = {=a}$; the $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$.
The branches lie in the {=br} regions formed by the asymptotes; the asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = {=-q}$; the $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$.
The branches lie in the {=brx} regions formed by the asymptotes; the asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = {=q}$; the $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$.
The branches lie in the {=br} regions formed by the asymptotes; the asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = {=x0}$; the $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$.

solution: Divide both sides by $x$ to reach the standard form $y = \frac{a}{x} + q$: $y = \frac{{=a}}{x} {=sg} {=abs(q)}$, so $a = {=a}$ and $q = {=q}$.
The sign of $a$ decides where the branches lie. Here $a$ is {=sgw}, so the branches lie in the {=br} regions formed by the asymptotes.
The vertical asymptote is $x = 0$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y = q$, that is $y = {=q}$.
For the $x$-intercept put $y = 0$: $\frac{{=a}}{x} = {=-q}$.
Multiply both sides by $x$ and divide by ${=-q}$: $x = {=a} \div ({=-q}) = {=x0}$, so the $x$-intercept is $({=x0}, 0)$. There is no $y$-intercept.
The correct description therefore has the branches in the {=br} regions, asymptotes $x = 0$ and $y = {=q}$, and $x$-intercept $({=x0}, 0)$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Puts the branches in the wrong pair of regions for the sign of a
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student reads the sign of a wrongly, often through a slip when rewriting xy = a + qx as y = a/x + q, and so places the branches in the pair of regions that belongs to the opposite sign of a, even though the asymptotes and intercept are right.

families.notes: Advanced tier: the book's own twist (the equation arrives as xy = ..., not y = a/x + q, as in ex6-8-57b) combined with the whole sketch method: sign of a, asymptotes, intercept. Each distractor changes exactly one component of the correct description and carries one named error; the require line makes the four wrong values differ from each other and from the correct one, so exactly one option is correct in every instance. The branch convention is the book's first/third versus second/fourth quadrant rule, restated relative to the point where the asymptotes cross (top-right and bottom-left for a > 0, top-left and bottom-right for a < 0); this was checked by x > 0 gives y > q when a > 0. |q| is at least 2 so the term q x never prints as 1x. x-intercept is x = -a/q and may be a fraction (rendered with \frac inside $...$, which is fine in an option); a is never 0. One proposed misconception is new (branches-sign-swapped); the other three ids are from the catalogue. The stem varies with a and q, so distinct_by_choices is not needed.

params.why: so that giving the numerator, or the opposite sign, can never coincide with the right asymptote

families.stem: The graph of ${=p}xy {=sg} {=abs(m)}x = {=c}$ is a hyperbola with horizontal asymptote $y = k$. Determine the value of $k$.
solution: To get $y$ on its own, first move the $x$-term to the right-hand side: ${=p}xy = {=c} {=sk} {=abs(m)}x$.
Divide every term by ${=p}x$: $y = \frac{{=c}}{{=p}x} {=sk} \frac{{=abs(m)}}{{=p}}$.
Simplify each fraction: $y = \frac{{=a}}{x} {=sk} {=abs(k)}$.
This has the form $y = \frac{a}{x} + q$ with $q = {=k}$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y = {=k}$ (the vertical asymptote is $x = 0$). Hence $k = {=k}$.
families.notes: Advanced tier: the book's twist from ex6-8-57b (the hyperbola is given as an xy-equation, not as y = a/x + q) with two extra steps the book's version does not need: the q-term starts on the left, so its sign must flip when it moves across (the asymptote-sign-flipped slip), and the whole equation carries a coefficient p on xy, so every term is divided by p x. Parameters make m = p*k and c = p*a exact multiples of p, so after dividing by p x the equation is y = a/x + k with whole numbers. |m| >= 2 so the x-term never prints as 1x; a and k are nonzero and |a| != |k|. The answer is the signed integer k, which is the book's 'the number added on the end', not the numerator a.

records.notes: Three families: one standard (x-intercept as a coordinate pair, from y = a/x + q) and two advanced (an mcq describing the whole sketch from the xy = a + qx form, and a numeric asymptote question from a coefficient-carrying xy-equation with the q-term on the left). The single book question (ex6-8-57b) is basic and only asks for the asymptote of xy = 3 + x, so the standard and advanced families extend the same y = a/x + q skeleton to the intercepts and the sign of a, which the objective names. The files were the only material I could open, so the families were not run through the engine. They rely on single-quoted string literals in let params and on string holes in templates; if the engine rejects strings, replace sg, br, brx and sgw with another device. One new misconception is proposed (branches-sign-swapped, in the describe family); the others use catalogue ids. Slug prefixes xinter, descri, rewrit are distinct.

families.stem: The graph of a hyperbolic function of the form $y=\dfrac{a}{x}+q$ has the horizontal asymptote $y={=q}$. Point A on the graph is at $\left({=x0}, {=y0}\right)$. Calculate the value of $a$.
solution: The horizontal asymptote of $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$ is the line $y=q$. Here the asymptote is $y={=q}$, so $q={=q}$.
Substitute $q={=q}$ and the coordinates of A, $x={=x0}$ and $y={=y0}$, into $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$: ${=y0}=\frac{a}{{=x0}}+{=q}$.
Multiply both sides by ${=x0}$ to clear the fraction: ${=x0}\times{=y0}=\left[\frac{a}{{=x0}}+{=q}\right]\times{=x0}$, so ${=xy}=a+{=qx}$.
Subtract ${=qx}$ from both sides: $a={=xy}-{=qx}={=a}$.
families.notes: Model: ex6-4-2 (A at (-1, 5), q = 3 from the dashed asymptote). The book's figure is replaced by a sentence naming the asymptote, which is exactly what the student reads off the dashed line; no figure is generated. Entry point of the skill: everything positive (a > 0, q > 0, x > 0), the point has whole-number coordinates, and only a is asked, q being read straight from the asymptote. x is never 1 so that 'multiply both sides by x' is never a vacuous step. a = k*x so y is always a whole number; a <= 15.

families.stem: The graph of a hyperbolic function of the form $y=\dfrac{a}{x}+q$ has the horizontal asymptote $y={=q}$. Point A on the graph is at $\left({=x0}, {=y0}\right)$. Calculate the values of $a$ and $q$.
solution: The horizontal asymptote of $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$ is the line $y=q$. Here the asymptote is $y={=q}$, so $q={=q}$.
Substitute $q={=q}$ and the coordinates of A, $x={=x0}$ and $y={=y0}$, into $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$: ${=y0}=\frac{a}{{=x0}}{=signed(q)}$.
Multiply both sides by ${=x0}$ to clear the fraction: $\left({=x0}\right)\times\left({=y0}\right)=\left[\frac{a}{{=x0}}{=signed(q)}\right]\times\left({=x0}\right)$, so ${=xy}=a{=signed(qx)}$.
Solve for $a$: $a={=xy}{=signed(-qx)}={=a}$.
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.
families.notes: The book's typical exercise (ex6-4-1, ex6-4-2, ex6-8-18), same method and the same two-value answer format as the book's own marker ('a = -1; q = 2'). The figure is replaced by a sentence naming the horizontal asymptote. x in {-2, -1, 2}, so y is a whole number or a half (as in ex6-4-1 with A(-2, 5/2)); a and q are non-zero whole numbers in [-4, 4]. x is never 1 so multiplying by x is never vacuous.

params.why: a is not a multiple of x, so the y-coordinate of A is a true fraction and the denominator has to be cleared

families.stem: The graph of a hyperbolic function of the form $y=\dfrac{a}{x}+q$ has the horizontal asymptote $y={=q}$. Point A on the graph is at $\left({=x0}, {=y0}\right)$. Calculate the values of $a$ and $q$.
solution: The horizontal asymptote of $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$ is the line $y=q$. Here the asymptote is $y={=q}$, so $q={=q}$.
Substitute $q={=q}$ and the coordinates of A, $x={=x0}$ and $y={=y0}$, into $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$: ${=y0}=\frac{a}{{=x0}}{=signed(q)}$.
Multiply both sides by ${=x0}$ to clear the fraction: $\left({=x0}\right)\times\left({=y0}\right)=\left[\frac{a}{{=x0}}{=signed(q)}\right]\times\left({=x0}\right)$, so ${=xy}=a{=signed(qx)}$.
Solve for $a$: $a={=xy}{=signed(-qx)}={=a}$.
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.
families.notes: Same skeleton as the standard family, at the book's harder end: A has a true fractional y-coordinate, the twist ex6-4-1 uses with A(-2, 5/2), but with x in {+-3, +-4, +-5} so the denominator to clear is 2, 3, 4 or 5, the multiplier is often negative, and a runs to 9 and q to 6 with either sign, so the product and the final subtraction carry signs. The book has no harder skeleton for this objective (all three of its questions use one asymptote and one point), so this is a step up in arithmetic, not in method. Answers a and q are whole numbers.

records.notes: Three families, one per tier, all on the book's own method: read q from the horizontal asymptote, substitute the point, multiply both sides by x, solve for a. The book questions show the graph as a figure (dashed asymptote labelled on the y-axis, point A marked). The families cannot generate a figure, so each stem states the asymptote y = q in words and gives A's coordinates. That is the same information the student reads off the dashed line. A reviewer may want to attach a rendered graph. The marker for the standard and advanced families copies the book's own format ("a = -1; q = 2", kind values, variables a and q). a and q are always whole numbers, so no fraction ever has to appear inside a plain marker answer. Fractions appear only in the point's y-coordinate in the stem, as in ex6-4-1. In the solution steps, {=signed(...)} is assumed to print an explicit + or - sign; if its output format differs, the steps still read as valid maths. The advanced tier is a harder-arithmetic variant (true fractional y, denominators 2 to 5, mixed signs, wider a and q). The book has no harder skeleton for this objective, so I did not invent a new method such as two points with no asymptote. I did not use mcq: the catalogue of misconceptions for this objective is empty and no choice is natural here. Candidate misconceptions a reviewer could add later: reading q as the y-coordinate of A, dropping the negative sign of x when substituting, and failing to multiply the constant q by x when clearing the fraction. I checked each family with a local simulation of 400 draws (math, constraints, template rendering). The distinct-stem counts were 60, 158 and 335.

families.stem: The graphs of $y={=b}^{x}$, $y={=c}^{x}$, $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=b}}\right)^{x}$ and $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=c}}\right)^{x}$ are drawn on the same system of axes. Which of these graphs has the greatest $y$-value at $x=-{=k}$?
solution: Substitute $x=-{=k}$ into each of the four equations.

$y=\left(\frac{1}{{=b}}\right)^{x}$ gives $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=b}}\right)^{-{=k}}={=b}^{{=k}}={=pb}$, and $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=c}}\right)^{x}$ gives $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=c}}\right)^{-{=k}}={=c}^{{=k}}={=pc}$.
Since ${=pc}>{=pb}>1>\frac{1}{{=pb}}>\frac{1}{{=pc}}$, the greatest value is ${=pc}$. So the graph of $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=c}}\right)^{x}$ is the highest at $x=-{=k}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Thinks the graph with the largest base is the highest at every x
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student turns 'a larger base makes a steeper graph' into 'a larger base makes a higher graph' and picks y = c^x at a negative x-value, where it is in fact the lowest of the four graphs.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ranks the two decreasing graphs by the size of their bases
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student knows that at a negative x-value the decreasing graphs y = (1/b)^x and y = (1/c)^x lie above 1, but picks the one with the larger base (1/b is bigger than 1/c) instead of working out that at negative x the smaller base gives the larger y-value.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Picks the rising graph with the smaller base for negative x
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student correctly sees that the order of the rising graphs reverses for negative x (b^x is above c^x there) but overlooks that both rising graphs are below 1 for negative x, so both decreasing graphs lie far above them.

families.notes: Advanced: a comparison of four graphs that the book draws in pairs (y = 2^x and y = (1/2)^x, Ex 6.5 Q6). It needs (1/b)^x = b^(-x) (the book's own step in 6c) and evaluation at a NEGATIVE x, where the order of the bases flips. Bases b < c are drawn from 2..5 (6 pairs) and k from 1..3, so there are 18 distinct stems; the stem always carries b, c and k so distinct_by_choices is not needed. The correct graph is always y = (1/c)^x, the other three distractors each correspond to one diagnosable error. All three misconception ids are new (the catalogued asymptote misconception does not apply to this question). No figure is needed: the stem is complete in words.

families.stem: The graphs of $y={=b}^{x}$ and $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=b}}\right)^{x}$ are drawn on the same system of axes. The point $P$ lies on the graph of $y={=b}^{x}$ and the point $Q$ lies on the graph of $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=b}}\right)^{x}$. Both points have $y$-coordinate ${=v}$. Calculate the length of $PQ$.
solution: Find the $x$-coordinate of $P$. Since ${=b}^{{=e}}={=v}$, the point $P$ is $({=e}, {=v})$.

The graph of $y=\left(\frac{1}{{=b}}\right)^{x}$ is the reflection of the graph of $y={=b}^{x}$ in the $y$-axis. So the point on it with the same $y$-coordinate is the reflection of $P$: $Q=({=-e}, {=v})$.
$P$ and $Q$ have the same $y$-coordinate, so $PQ$ is horizontal and its length is the difference between the $x$-coordinates: $PQ={=n}-(-{=n})={=2 * n}$.
families.notes: Advanced: uses the objective's key comparison (y = (1/b)^x is the reflection of y = b^x in the y-axis) in several steps: read x from a y-value using the powers of b (a table-of-values step, including negative exponents when v < 1), reflect, then find a horizontal distance. b is drawn from 2..5 with exponent size n capped so that v stays a small clean power (at most 125) or its reciprocal; the sign of the exponent is random, so v is either a whole number or a unit fraction (rendered as \frac). There are 22 distinct stems. The answer is always 2n, a whole number. Because y = b^x is one-to-one, P and Q are unique. No figure is needed; the book figure for the parent (ex6-8-48d) shows y = 2^x and y = -2^x, which this family does not use.

families.stem: The graphs of $f(x)={=b}^{x}$ and $g(x)=-{=a}x^{2}+q$ are drawn on the same system of axes. Both graphs pass through the point $A$ on the $y$-axis. The point $B$ lies on the graph of $f$ and the point $C$ lies on the graph of $g$; both points have $x$-coordinate ${=m}$. Calculate the length of $BC$.
solution: $f(0)={=b}^{0}=1$, so $A=(0, 1)$. (Every graph of the form $y=b^{x}$ passes through $(0, 1)$.)
$B$ and $C$ have the same $x$-coordinate, so $BC$ is vertical and $BC={=fb}-({=gm})={=fb - gm}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own twist from Ex 6.8 Q50 (f(x) = 4^x and g(x) = -4x^2 + q meeting at A(0, 1), with B on f and C on g above the same x). The only exponential-graph fact needed is the common y-intercept (0, 1), which fixes q; g is then only evaluated, never analysed, so no quadratic-graph technique beyond substitution is used. The stem is written out in words, so the book's figure is not needed (it was read: it shows f, g, A on the y-axis, B on f, C on g, with BC vertical and dashed). b and a are drawn from 2..5 (a >= 2 avoids a printed coefficient of 1) and m from 1..2, giving 32 distinct stems with answers 5 to 44. g(m) = 1 - a m^2 is always negative, so C is always below B and the subtraction is always B minus C with brackets. Reviewers: if quadratics are judged out of scope for this objective, drop this family; the other two stand without it.

records.notes: Only the advanced tier was a gap, so three advanced families were written, each with its own solution skeleton and a different slug prefix (highes, mirror, quadex): a four-graph mcq comparison at a negative x, a reflection-distance numeric, and the book's exponential-plus-quadratic twist. Both book figures were read. All parameter ranges were checked in a scratch script: 18, 22 and 32 distinct stems, every answer a whole number, no ties in the mcq, and C always below B. A basic or standard family was not added because those tiers were not listed as gaps, and the objective offers no honest fourth advanced skeleton that would not just repeat the reflection idea.

params.why: keeps the height of the second point small

families.stem: The graph of the exponential function $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}+q$, with $b>0$, has the horizontal asymptote $y={=q}$. The graph cuts the $y$-axis at the point $A(0, {=p})$ and passes through the point $B({=n}, {=r})$. Determine the equation of $f$, in the form $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}+q$.
solution: The horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}+q$ is the line $y=q$. The asymptote is $y={=q}$, so $q={=q}$ and $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Substitute the $y$-intercept $A(0, {=p})$. Since $b^{0}=1$, we get ${=p}=a\cdot b^{0} {=qop} {=qabs}$, so ${=p}=a {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Solve for $a$: $a={=p} {=qneg} {=qabs}={=a}$. So $f(x)={=a}\cdot b^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Substitute the point $B({=n}, {=r})$: ${=r}={=a}\cdot b^{{=n}} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Isolate the power of $b$: ${=r} {=qneg} {=qabs}={=a}\cdot b^{{=n}}$, so ${=d}={=a}\cdot b^{{=n}}$. Divide by ${=a}$: $b^{{=n}}=\frac{{=d}}{{=a}}={=pw}$.
Since $b>0$ and ${=pw}={=b}^{{=n}}$, we have $b={=b}$.
Therefore $f(x)={=a}\cdot {=b}^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
families.notes: Text-only restatement of the book's ex6-5-7a figure (asymptote, y-intercept A, second point B). The book's figure shows the asymptote as a dashed line, so the stem states it; b>0 is stated so b is unique. Twist beyond ex6-5-7a: the asymptote is not the x-axis (q is never 0) and a is not 1, so the student reads q from the asymptote, finds a from the y-intercept, and only then finds b from the second point (three unknowns). Method is exactly the book's: q from the asymptote, then substitute points. Parameters: b in {2,3}, second point at x=2 or 3, a in +-1..3, q in -5..5 excluding 0, |a*b^n| <= 30, giving 200 distinct instances. Because a and b^n are both positive when b>0, the sign of a decides whether the curve lies above or below its asymptote (sign-of-a-lost is the typical wrong answer when the point A lies below the asymptote). The sign of q is rendered through let-params qop/qneg holding '+' or '-' (string literals); if the engine refuses string literals in let, replace them with signed(q).

families.stem: The graph of the exponential function $f(x)=a\cdot 2^{x}+q$ has the horizontal asymptote $y={=q}$ and passes through the point $A(-{=m}, {=vd})$. The graph of $g$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the $x$-axis. Determine the equation of $g$, in the form $g(x)=c\cdot 2^{x}+d$.
solution: The horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=a\cdot 2^{x}+q$ is the line $y=q$. The asymptote is $y={=q}$, so $q={=q}$ and $f(x)=a\cdot 2^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Substitute the point $A(-{=m}, {=vd})$: ${=vd}=a\cdot 2^{-{=m}} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Isolate the power of $2$: ${=vd} {=qneg} {=qabs}=a\cdot 2^{-{=m}}$. Since $2^{-{=m}}={=wd}$, this gives ${=dd}=a\cdot({=wd})$.
Divide by ${=wd}$: $a=\frac{{=dd}}{{=wd}}={=a}$.
So $f(x)={=a}\cdot 2^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Reflecting in the $x$-axis replaces every $y$-value by its negative, so $g(x)=-f(x)=-\left({=a}\cdot 2^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}\right)$.
Remove the brackets: $g(x)={=na}\cdot 2^{x} {=gop} {=gabs}$. Both $a$ and $q$ change sign, so the asymptote of $g$ is $y={=gq}$.
families.notes: Joins two of the book's steps: finding a and q from the asymptote and one point near it on y=a*2^x+q (ex6-5-2, ex6-5-3, ex6-8-25, which use A(-3, 3.875), A(-3, 4.875), A(-3, -3.625)) and writing the equation of the reflection in the x-axis (ex6-5-7b). With a=-1,q=4,m=3 the stem reproduces ex6-5-2; with a=3,q=-4,m=3 it reproduces ex6-8-25. The point is given as an exact decimal (multiples of 0.125, 0.25 or 0.5), so no rounding instruction is needed and a, q are integers. The twist is that a reflection in the x-axis negates the WHOLE function: the asymptote moves from y=q to y=-q, so q changes sign as well as a. The book only reflects 3^x (q=0); the technique (negate f) is the same. Typical wrong answers: -a*2^x + q (keeps q; not catalogued), a*2^(-x) + q (reflection-axes-swapped), or a wrong-signed a (sign-of-a-lost). Reflection in the x-axis is chosen deliberately instead of vertical stretch: a vertical stretch of a function with q not 0 is ambiguous (does the asymptote move?), and the book never states it for q not 0. Parameters: m in {1,2,3}, a in +-1..4, q in -5..5 excluding 0, giving 240 distinct instances. Signs of q are rendered through let-params holding '+' or '-' (string literals); if the engine refuses string literals in let, replace them with signed(...).

records.notes: Two advanced families, both text-only restatements of the book's figures (the figure's dashed asymptote is stated in the stem). Gap list named only the advanced tier, so no basic or standard family was written; the book questions already serve the standard tier. Vertical stretch was deliberately not used on functions with q not 0 because the book never defines it there and the wording is ambiguous (does the asymptote move?). Both families use string let-params for the sign of q ('+' / '-'); if the engine rejects string literals, swap them for signed(...). Decimals in the F2 stem go through float(...) so they print as 3.875, not as a fraction.

families.stem: Determine the domain and range of $f(x) = {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$. Which of the following is correct?
solution: The power ${=b}^x$ can be calculated for every real number $x$, so there is no restriction on $x$: the domain is $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
Compare $f(x) = {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$ with $y = ab^x + q$: here $a = 1$, which is positive, and $q = {=q}$.
Because $a > 0$, the power ${=b}^x$ is positive for every $x$, so $f(x) = {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$ is always greater than ${=q}$: the graph lies above the line $y = {=q}$.
The graph gets closer and closer to $y = {=q}$ but never reaches it, so ${=q}$ is not part of the range. The range is $y \in ({=q}, \infty)$, with a round bracket.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ignores q: takes y = 0 as the boundary of the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student states the range of y = ab^x + q as (0, infinity) or (-infinity, 0), forgetting that q moves the boundary line from y = 0 to y = q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Puts the range on the wrong side of y = q
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student gives (-infinity, q) when a is positive, or (q, infinity) when a is negative, instead of using the sign of a to decide whether the graph lies above or below y = q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Includes y = q in the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student writes a square bracket, [q, infinity) or (-infinity, q], as if the graph reached the line y = q. It only gets closer and closer, so the bracket must be round.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Swaps domain and range
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student restricts x by the boundary value q and says every real number is an output, the wrong way round: for an exponential the domain is all real numbers and the range is restricted.

families.notes: Basic entry point, modelled on the book's y = 2^x range with a vertical shift q added. a is fixed at 1 so the family has one skeleton (range above y = q); the opposite direction is practised in the standard and advanced families and appears here as a distractor. q is never 0 so that the 'range from zero' and 'swapped' options stay distinct from the key. mcq because the answer is an interval with infinity: every distractor is a named error. The domain is always R for y = ab^x + q.

families.stem: Consider $f(x) = {=a}\cdot {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$ and $g(x) = -{=a}\cdot {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$. Which of the following gives the range of $f$ and the range of $g$?
solution: For $f(x) = {=a}\cdot {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$ read off $a = {=a}$, which is positive, and $q = {=q}$.
Since $a > 0$, ${=a}\cdot {=b}^x$ is positive for every $x$, so $f(x) > {=q}$. The graph never reaches $y = {=q}$, so the range of $f$ is $y \in ({=q}, \infty)$.
For $g(x) = -{=a}\cdot {=b}^x{=signed(q)}$ read off $a = -{=a}$, which is negative, and $q = {=q}$.

families.stem: Exactly one of the following exponential functions has no $x$-intercept. Which one?
solution: To find an $x$-intercept we let $y=0$. For $y=a\cdot b^{x}+q$ this gives $a\cdot b^{x}=-q$, so $b^{x}=-\frac{q}{a}$.
A power of a positive base is always positive. So there is an $x$-intercept only if $-\frac{q}{a}$ is positive; if it is negative, the equation has no solution.
For $y={=a1}\cdot {=b1}^{x}{=signed(q1)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b1}^{x}={=c1}$. This is positive, so there is an $x$-intercept.
For $y={=a2}\cdot {=b2}^{x}{=signed(q2)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b2}^{x}={=c2}$. This is positive, so there is an $x$-intercept.
For $y={=a3}\cdot {=b3}^{x}{=signed(q3)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b3}^{x}={=c3}$. This is positive, so there is an $x$-intercept.
For $y={=a0}\cdot {=b0}^{x}{=signed(q0)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b0}^{x}={=c0}$. This is negative, and no power of ${=b0}$ is negative, so there is no solution.
The function with no $x$-intercept is $y={=a0}\cdot {=b0}^{x}{=signed(q0)}$.

families.stem: The graph of $y = {=a}\sin\theta {=qs} {=qa}$ is sketched for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. What is the $y$-value of the turning point at $\theta = 270^\circ$?
solution: On the basic graph $y = \sin\theta$ the turning point at $\theta = 270^\circ$ is the minimum, where $y = -1$.
Multiplying by $a = {=a}$ stretches the graph vertically by a factor of ${=abs(a)}$, and $a$ {=refl}. The point at $\theta = 270^\circ$ therefore moves to $y = {=a} \times (-1) = {=-a}$.
The shift $q = {=q}$ moves every point {=dir} ${=qa}$ units, so $y = {=-a} {=qs} {=qa} = {=q - a}$.
The turning point at $\theta = 270^\circ$ has $y = {=q - a}$.
families.notes: Standard: read one turning point of y = a sin θ + q from the effects of a (stretch, and reflection when a is negative) and q (shift). Check: a sin 270° + q = q - a, so the answer is q - a for every instance. The sign of a is mixed on purpose so the reflection (the turning point at 270° becomes a maximum) is tested. Zero answers are excluded (q != a). Let-strings contain no backslashes; they use plain words so no escape sequence can be misread.

families.stem: Consider the graph of $y = {=a}\sin\theta {=qs} {=qa}$ for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. Which option correctly gives its amplitude and its range?
solution: The basic graph $y = \sin\theta$ has amplitude $1$ and range $-1 \le y \le 1$.

Here $a = {=a}$ is negative, so the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis and stretched vertically by a factor of ${=b}$. An amplitude is a distance, so it is ${=b}$, not ${=a}$. The graph of $y = {=a}\sin\theta$ runs from ${=-b}$ to ${=b}$.

The shift $q = {=q}$ moves every point {=dir} ${=qa}$ units. It is added after the stretch, so it is not multiplied by $a$. The lowest value is ${=-b} {=qs} {=qa} = {=lo}$ and the highest value is ${=b} {=qs} {=qa} = {=hi}$.
The amplitude is ${=b}$ and the range is ${=lo} \le y \le {=hi}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Leaves the vertical shift out of the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds the range of a sin θ correctly, from -|a| to |a|, but forgets that q moves the highest and lowest values, so the range is left centred on the x-axis.

families.notes: Standard: describe the effect of a and q on y = a sin θ + q. a is always negative so the reflection is always present and the catalogued negative-amplitude error is a genuine, distinguishable option. Each option is an (amplitude, range) pair, all four are distinct for every instance (q is never 0 and |a| >= 2, so the stretch-applied-to-shift range a*q ± |a| differs from both the correct range and the unshifted one). Range is over a full period, 0° to 360°. The stem has {=...} holes so instances differ by their numbers; distinct_by_choices is not needed. Let-strings contain no backslashes.

params.name: sgn
params.let: 'positive, so the graph is not reflected' if a > 0 else 'negative, so the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis'

families.stem: The graph of $y = a\sin\theta + q$ is sketched for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. Its two turning points are $(90^\circ, {=p})$ and $(270^\circ, {=r})$. Which equation does the graph have?
solution: The turning points give the greatest and least values of $y$: $y_{\max} = {=mx}$ and $y_{\min} = {=mn}$.
The amplitude is half the distance between them: $|a| = \frac{{=mx} - ({=mn})}{2} = {=b}$.
The middle line of the graph lies halfway between the greatest and least values, and that height is the vertical shift: $q = \frac{{=mx} + ({=mn})}{2} = {=q}$.

At $\theta = 90^\circ$ the basic sine graph is at its highest point. Here the value ${=p}$ at $\theta = 90^\circ$ is {=rel} than the value ${=r}$ at $\theta = 270^\circ$, so $a$ is {=sgn}. Therefore $a = {=a}$.
The equation is $y = {=a}\sin\theta {=qs} {=qa}$. Check: at $\theta = 90^\circ$, $y = {=a} \times 1 {=qs} {=qa} = {=p}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gets the sign of a (the reflection) the wrong way round
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds |a| and q correctly but decides which turning point is the maximum the wrong way, so they write a positive a for a graph that is reflected in the x-axis, or a negative a for one that is not.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the distance between the turning points as a
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student subtracts the lowest value from the highest value and uses the whole height, 2|a|, as the stretch factor instead of halving it to get the amplitude.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gets the direction of the vertical shift wrong
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds the size of the shift but writes the opposite sign for q, so a graph shifted up is written as shifted down and the other way round.

families.notes: Advanced: match an equation to a graph described by its two turning points (no figure is needed). Turning points are always (90°, a+q) and (270°, q-a), so p > r exactly when a > 0. a mixes signs so the reflection step is tested. |a| >= 2, q != 0 and the three distractors are each a single error (sign of a, size of a, sign of q), so all four options are distinct for every instance; the correct option is never equal to a distractor. Stem holes (p, r) make instances differ. Let-strings contain no backslashes.

params.why: the graph is then genuinely shifted and q is a non-zero shift

params.name: note
params.let: 'Check: $a$ is negative, so the graph is reflected and its lowest point is at 90 degrees, which is why this value equals the given minimum.' if a < 0 else 'Check: $a$ is positive, so the graph is not reflected and its highest point is at 90 degrees, which is why this value is above the given minimum.'

families.stem: For $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$, the graph of $y = {=a}\sin\theta + q$ has a minimum value of ${=m}$. Determine the value of $y$ when $\theta = 90^\circ$.
solution: Without the shift, $y = {=a}\sin\theta$ is the basic sine graph stretched by a factor of ${=b}$ (its amplitude is ${=b}$ whether $a$ is positive or negative), so it runs from ${=-b}$ to ${=b}$.
The shift $q$ moves the lowest value to $-{=b} + q$. This is the given minimum, so $-{=b} + q = {=m}$ and $q = {=m} + {=b} = {=q}$.
At $\theta = 90^\circ$, $\sin 90^\circ = 1$, so $y = {=a} \times 1 {=qs} {=qa} = {=a + q}$.
{=note}
families.notes: Advanced: the twist is the reflection. The minimum of y = a sin θ + q is q - |a| whether a is positive or negative, so q = m + |a|. Then y(90°) = a + q: for a < 0 this equals m (the lowest point moves to 90°), for a > 0 it is m + 2a. One skeleton covers both signs. q = 0 is excluded so every instance has a real shift. Verified numerically over a full period for every parameter pair. Let-strings contain no backslashes; the final step is a plain-words check.

records.notes: Book questions for this objective are all basic (match f, g, h, k to y = a sin θ for a = 1, 1/2, 3, 2 from a figure). Two standard and two advanced families written, all text-only so no figure is needed: standard = turning-point value at 270° (numeric) and amplitude-and-range mcq using the catalogued negative-amplitude and stretch-applied-to-shift misconceptions plus one new one; advanced = match an equation from two turning points (mcq, three new single-error distractors) and find y at 90° from a given minimum (numeric, reflection twist). Every parameter set was enumerated outside the engine: answers are right, options are distinct, and there are at least 32 distinct instances per family. All let-strings avoid backslashes. They use single-quoted string literals for sign and wording choices (e.g. '+' if q > 0 else '-'); if the engine accepts only double-quoted literals, swap the quotes.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta)={=a}\sin\theta {=signed(q)}$ is drawn for $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$. What is the amplitude of $f$?
solution: For $f(\theta)=a\sin\theta+q$ the amplitude is $|a|$: the distance from the middle line $y=q$ up to the maximum (or down to the minimum). It is never negative, and $q$ only moves the graph up or down, so it does not change the amplitude.
Here $a={=a}$, so the amplitude is $|{=a}|={=abs(a)}$.
families.notes: Entry point: read a off the equation. a is negative in half of the instances (the book's own f(x) = -sin x + 2 has amplitude 1, not -1) and q is always non-zero so the equation prints with a sign. Answer is |a|; q is the decoy. Params give 100 distinct instances.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta)={=a}\sin\theta {=signed(q)}$ is drawn for $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$. Write down the coordinates of the minimum turning point of $f$ in the form $(\theta, y)$, with $\theta$ in degrees (do not write the degree sign).
solution: Because $a={=a}$ is positive, the graph starts on the middle line $y={=q}$, rises to its maximum at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and falls to its minimum at $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
At $\theta=270^{\circ}$, $\sin270^{\circ}=-1$, so $f(270^{\circ})={=a}\times(-1) {=signed(q)}={=q - a}$.
The minimum turning point is $(270, {=q - a})$.
families.notes: Standard: a > 0 only (reflection is the advanced family). The minimum is at 270 degrees, with y = q - a (the book's 3 sin(theta) has it at (270, -3)). a in 2..6 and q non-zero in -5..5 give 50 instances. The stem fixes the degree convention so a blind solver does not add a degree sign.

params.why: keeps every option different from the correct range

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta)={=a}\sin\theta {=signed(q)}$ is drawn for $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$. Which of the following is the range of $f$?
solution: For every angle, $-1\le\sin\theta\le1$.
Multiply every part by $a={=a}$. It is positive, so the inequality signs keep their direction: $-{=a}\le {=a}\sin\theta\le {=a}$.
Add $q={=q}$ to every part. The lowest value is $-{=a} {=signed(q)}={=q - a}$ and the highest value is ${=a} {=signed(q)}={=q + a}$.
So the range is ${=q - a}\le f(\theta)\le {=q + a}$: the graph is centred on the middle line $y={=q}$ and reaches $a={=a}$ units above and below it.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ignores the vertical shift q in the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives -a <= f <= a, the range of a sin(theta), as if q = 0. The graph of a sin(theta) + q is the same graph moved q units up or down, so both ends of the range move by q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Moves the range the wrong way
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives -a - q <= f <= a - q: takes + q to mean a shift of q units in the opposite direction, so a positive q lowers the range and a negative q raises it.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ignores the amplitude a in the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives q - 1 <= f <= q + 1: shifts the range -1 <= sin(theta) <= 1 by q but forgets that a stretches it, so the distance from the middle line to the turning points is a, not 1.

families.notes: Standard: describe the range of a sin(theta) + q with a > 0. Each distractor is one named error. a in 2..6, q non-zero in -5..5, a != q: 46 instances; the check in Python confirmed the four options are always distinct and each has lower < upper. The stem has holes for a and q, so distinct_by_choices is not set.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta)=a\sin\theta+q$ is drawn for $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$. It cuts the $y$-axis at $(0, {=q0})$ and its minimum turning point is at $(90^{\circ}, {=m})$. What is the maximum value of $f$?
solution: Since $\sin0^{\circ}=0$, $f(0^{\circ})=q$, so the $y$-intercept gives $q={=q0}$.
Since $\sin90^{\circ}=1$, $f(90^{\circ})=a+q$. With $q={=q0}$ and $f(90^{\circ})={=m}$ we get $a={=m}-({=q0})={=m - q0}$.

The value of $a$ is negative, so this is a reflected sine graph: it falls from the middle line $y={=q0}$ to its minimum at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and rises to its maximum at $\theta=270^{\circ}$. The amplitude is $|a|={=d}$.
The maximum value of $f$ is ${=q0 + d}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own twist (figure of ex6-8-46c is f(x) = -sin x + 2, with minimum A at 90 degrees and y-intercept 2). The minimum turning point sitting at 90 degrees forces a < 0; the student must find q from the y-intercept, a from the turning point, then the maximum at 270 degrees. Answer is q0 + d (equivalently 2*q0 - m). Brute-force check over all 40 instances confirmed the maximum and the minimum position. q0 in -3..4, d in 1..5.

records.notes: Four families: basic (amplitude), standard (minimum turning point, range mcq), advanced (reflected sine: find the maximum from the y-intercept and the minimum at 90 degrees). The book's standard questions here (positive, increasing, decreasing on a drawn sine/cosine graph) would give the same interval answer for every instance, so I did not write an interval family for them. Domain and period are constant (0 to 360 degrees, 360 degrees), so no honest family exists for them. x-intercepts with q different from 0 need trig equations (a neighbouring objective), so intercepts appear only as the y-intercept (0, q) in the advanced family. Assumes signed(q) prints with its sign for non-zero q; q is never zero where signed is used. All answers were brute-force checked in Python; the engine itself was not run.

families.stem: Let $f(\theta) = a\cos\theta + q$, where $a = {=a}$ and $q = {=q}$. The graph of $f$ is drawn for $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 360^\circ$. Which of the following is the range of $f$?
solution: For $y = \cos\theta$ the highest value is $1$ and the lowest value is $-1$.
Multiplying by $a = {=a}$ stretches the graph, so the amplitude is $|a| = {=a}$ and $a\cos\theta$ runs from ${=0 - a}$ up to ${=a}$.
Adding $q = {=q}$ moves every point of the graph up by $q$ units (down if $q$ is negative), so the lowest value is $q - a = {=q - a}$ and the highest value is $q + a = {=q + a}$.
The range is ${=q - a} \leq f(\theta) \leq {=q + a}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Forgets the vertical shift q when stating the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives the range of a cos θ, from -a to a, without moving it up or down by q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Forgets the amplitude a when stating the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: Shifts the range of cos θ, from -1 to 1, by q but does not stretch it by the factor a.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Moves the range the wrong way for q
proposed_misconceptions.description: Subtracts q from both ends of the range of a cos θ, so a positive q moves the graph down and a negative q moves it up.

families.notes: The book items of this objective read the amplitude off a drawn graph (two of them, 6-19c and 6-20c, have q not zero and a negative); no figure can be sampled, so the family asks for the range of a given f(θ) = a cos θ + q on 0 to 360 degrees. Range is written as an inequality, not interval notation, so no bracket or separator convention can mismatch. a is positive here (the reflected case is in the advanced families); q is never 0 and a is at least 2, so the four options are always different (D1 equals the correct option only if q = 0, D2 only if a = 1, D3 only if q = 0). The engine's range convention is the book's: lowest value q - |a|, highest value q + |a|.

families.stem: To plot the graph of $f(\theta) = a\cos\theta + q$ for $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 360^\circ$, where $a = {=a}$ and $q = {=q}$, a table of values is completed with a calculator. What is the value of $f({=th}^\circ)$ in the table?
solution: Use a calculator to find $\cos {=th}^\circ = {=fixed(c2 / 2, 1)}$.
Multiply by $a$: $a\cos {=th}^\circ = {=a} \times ({=fixed(c2 / 2, 1)}) = {=fa}$.
Add $q = {=q}$ to get $f({=th}^\circ) = a\cos {=th}^\circ + q = {=fa + q}$.
families.notes: Table-of-values step of the objective (the plotting skill), restated as a single value because the book's own items are graph-reading and cannot be sampled. Angles are limited to 60, 120, 240 and 300 degrees, where the calculator gives cos = 0.5 or -0.5 exactly, and a is always an even whole number (a = 2sm), so every answer is a whole number with no rounding. a may be negative (the reflected cosine the book uses in exercise 6.8). q is never 0. 4 x 2 x 10 x 4 = 320 distinct instances.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta) = a\cos\theta + q$ is drawn for $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 360^\circ$. It passes through the point $(0^\circ, {=v0})$ and has a turning point at $(180^\circ, {=v180})$. Find the value of $a$.
solution: Use $\cos 0^\circ = 1$ and $\cos 180^\circ = -1$: $f(0^\circ) = a + q$ and $f(180^\circ) = -a + q$.
The two given points say $a + q = {=v0}$ and $-a + q = {=v180}$.
Subtract the second equation from the first: $2a = f(0^\circ) - f(180^\circ) = {=v0 - v180}$.
Divide by 2: $a = {=a}$.

Check: the highest and lowest values of the graph are ${=abs(v0 - v180)}$ units apart, so the amplitude is half of that, ${=m}$, and this equals $|a|$. A positive $a$ makes the graph start at its highest point and a negative $a$ makes it start at its lowest point.
families.notes: Twist taken from the book's own graph in 6-8-47c, g(x) = -3cos x + 1 (starts at its lowest point, amplitude 3 although the maximum is 4): the sign of a has to be found as well as the amplitude. Sampled over a positive and a negative a (|a| from 2 to 6), q never 0, so v0 differs from v180 and a is always a whole number. The solution uses only cos 0 = 1 and cos 180 = -1, the values on the plotted table, then the book's amplitude idea as a check. 5 x 2 x 10 = 100 instances.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta) = a\cos\theta + q$ is drawn for $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 360^\circ$. Its range is ${=lo} \leq f(\theta) \leq {=hi}$, and the graph starts (at $\theta = 0^\circ$) at its lowest point. Find the value of $f(60^\circ)$.
solution: The highest and lowest values are ${=hi - lo}$ units apart, and the amplitude is half of that: $|a| = {=amp}$.
The graph is centred half-way between its lowest and highest values: $q = \frac{{=lo + hi}}{2} = {=q}$.
The graph starts at its lowest point, so the cosine graph has been turned upside down: $a$ is negative and $a = {=0 - amp}$.
Use a calculator: $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$, so $a\cos 60^\circ = {=0 - amp} \times 0.5 = {=0 - k}$.
families.notes: Several-step item in the spirit of the book's amplitude questions 6-19c and 6-20c, where the amplitude is half the distance between the highest and lowest values, not the maximum itself, and q is the centre line. Here the range is given instead of a drawn graph, the sign of a comes from 'starts at its lowest point' (always a negative), and the final step is a calculator value for the table, cos 60 = 0.5. a = -2k is always even, so f(60) = q - k is always a whole number. q is never 0. 4 x 10 = 40 instances.

records.notes: Both listed gaps are filled: two standard families (an mcq on the range, where the three distractors map to the new ids mc:g10m6s6-2-1:range-ignores-q, range-ignores-a and range-shift-wrong-way, and a numeric table-of-values entry) and two advanced families (finding a, with its sign, from f(0 degrees) and the turning point at 180 degrees, and a multi-step item that goes from the range and start-at-lowest to f(60 degrees)). The four book questions are graph-reading amplitude items whose figures I viewed, with no figure that can be sampled, so each family restates the same skill in words and numbers. The function is stated by giving a and q as separate values so that no sign-handling helper is needed in the stems. Slug prefixes are rangep, tablev, findas and midlin. The turning point asked about is always the one at 180 degrees, to avoid the ambiguity of the end points of the closed domain. Solving a cos(theta) + q = 0 for x-intercepts was left out as it needs the inverse cosine and a second solution, which the book's method for this objective does not use. Intercepts reached only through f(0 degrees).

params.name: q
params.resample_while: q == 0 or q == a or q == 2 * a

families.stem: A learner sketches $y = {=a}\cos\theta {=signed(q)}$ for $\theta \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ]$ without a table of values, by working out the points of the sketch at $\theta = 0^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. Which option gives these three points correctly?
solution: The graph of $y = \cos\theta$ passes through $(0^\circ, 1)$, $(180^\circ, -1)$ and $(360^\circ, 1)$. Multiplying by $a$ stretches these heights (and reflects them in the $x$-axis when $a < 0$); adding $q$ shifts every point vertically by $q$.
At $\theta = 0^\circ$, $\cos\theta = 1$, so $y = {=a}\cdot 1 {=signed(q)} = {=a + q}$.
At $\theta = 180^\circ$, $\cos\theta = -1$, so $y = {=a}\cdot(-1) {=signed(q)} = {=q - a}$.
At $\theta = 360^\circ$, $\cos\theta$ is $1$ again, so $y = {=a + q}$ again.
The points are $(0^\circ, {=a + q})$, $(180^\circ, {=q - a})$ and $(360^\circ, {=a + q})$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Getting the reflection in the x-axis the wrong way round
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student swaps the heights at 0 and 360 degrees with the height at 180 degrees: for a negative a they ignore the reflection and start the sketch at its maximum as for y = cos theta (and for a positive a they start it at its minimum), so the two turning heights q + a and q - a trade places.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Leaving out the vertical shift q
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student plots the points of y = a cos theta and forgets to add q, so the sketch is centred on the x-axis instead of on the line y = q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Shifting the graph the wrong way
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student applies the shift with the wrong sign, subtracting q instead of adding it, so a graph shifted up is drawn shifted down and the other way round.

families.notes: Standard: the three key points of the sketch (0, 180, 360 degrees), which is how a sketch is built without a table. Every instance has a != 0, q != 0, q != a, q != 2a, which makes the four options differ in their first coordinate pair (checked over the whole parameter space: 56 instances, all with four distinct options). The correct option is a+q, q-a, a+q; the swapped option is the reflection error in either direction. For a < 0 the correct option starts at the minimum. Coordinates are (angle, y). Parent is a basic book item; no book question asks for the key points of a sketch, so this extends the book's amplitude identification to the full a and q effect.

families.stem: Sketch the graph of $y = {=a}\cos\theta {=signed(q)}$ for $\theta \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ]$ without using a table of values. What is the least value of $y$ on your sketch?
solution: The amplitude is $|a| = {=abs(a)}$: the graph of $y = \cos\theta$ is stretched vertically so that it rises ${=abs(a)}$ above, and falls ${=abs(a)}$ below, its midline.
The vertical shift $q = {=q}$ moves the whole graph, so its midline is the line $y = {=q}$.
The least value is the midline minus the amplitude: ${=q} - {=abs(a)} = {=q - abs(a)}$.

The sign of $a$ only decides where this lowest point is: at $\theta = 180^\circ$ when $a > 0$, and at $\theta = 0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ when $a < 0$ (the reflection in the $x$-axis). It does not change the value.
The least value of $y$ is ${=q - abs(a)}$.
families.notes: Standard: range reasoning from amplitude and shift. a runs over both signs so the student must use |a|, not a, for the distance from the midline: least value = q - |a| in every case (verified numerically over the whole parameter space against the sampled curve). |a| >= 2 so the coefficient always prints as a number; q != 0 so the shift always prints. Answer is a whole number, possibly negative.

families.stem: The graph of $y = a\cos\theta + q$ is sketched for $\theta \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ]$. On this interval the greatest value of $y$ is ${=top}$ and the least value of $y$ is ${=bot}$, and the graph passes through the point $(0^\circ, {=k})$. Find the value of $a$.
solution: The graph oscillates between its least value ${=bot}$ and its greatest value ${=top}$, so its midline $y = q$ is halfway between them: $q = ({=top} + {=paren(bot)}) \div 2 = {=q}$.
The amplitude is the distance from the midline to the greatest value: $|a| = {=top} - {=paren(q)} = {=amp}$.
At $\theta = 0^\circ$, $\cos\theta = 1$, so $y = a + q$ there. The graph passes through $(0^\circ, {=k})$, so $a + {=paren(q)} = {=k}$.

So $a = {=k} - {=paren(q)} = {=a}$. This agrees with $|a| = {=amp}$, and its sign shows the reflection: $a$ is positive when the graph starts at its greatest value and negative when it starts at its least value.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own inverse problem (read a and q off the features of a graph, here given in words because the stem cannot carry a diagram) with the twist that the sign of a must be decided from where the graph starts. Half the instances have a > 0 (the point at 0 degrees is the greatest value), half a < 0 (it is the least value); a is a whole number from -6 to 6, never 0, and q is a whole number, never 0. Checked numerically over the whole parameter space: greatest and least values of the sampled curve equal q + |a| and q - |a|, midline (top+bot)/2 = q, amplitude top - q = |a|, and k - q = a. The data are consistent and determine a uniquely.

families.stem: Sketch the graph of $y = {=a}\cos\theta {=signed(q)}$ for $\theta \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ]$ without using a table of values. How many $x$-intercepts does your sketch have?
solution: The amplitude is $|a| = {=abs(a)}$ and the vertical shift is $q = {=q}$, so the midline is the line $y = {=q}$.
The graph therefore lies between its least value ${=q - abs(a)}$ and its greatest value ${=q + abs(a)}$.

The $x$-axis is the line $y = 0$. The graph cuts it only if $0$ lies strictly between the least and the greatest value, which happens exactly when $|q| < |a|$, that is when the shift is smaller than the amplitude. Then the graph crosses the axis once on the way down and once on the way up. If $|q| > |a|$ the whole graph stays on one side of the axis and never reaches it.
Here $|q| = {=abs(q)}$ and $|a| = {=abs(a)}$.
So the sketch has ${=ans}$ $x$-intercepts.
families.notes: Advanced: combines the effect of a (amplitude) with the effect of q (shift) to decide whether the sketch reaches the x-axis. The case |q| = |a| (graph only touches the axis, at 0 and 360 degrees or at 180 degrees) is excluded so the answer is unambiguous; q = 0 is excluded so the shift always prints. Answer is 2 when |q| < |a| and 0 when |q| > |a|; both occur equally often over the parameter space (40 each; verified by counting sign changes of the sampled curve). Intercepts are interior points of the interval, so the count does not depend on how the end points are treated.

records.notes: Both gaps (standard, advanced) filled with two families each. The book's four items for this objective are all basic (match a graph to y = a cos theta, figure with f, g, h, k), so the new families extend them to the full a and q effect on a sketch for theta in [0, 360] degrees: key points (mcq with named errors), least value, recovering a from described features (sign decided from the y-intercept), and counting x-intercepts. Every numeric answer is a whole number; every mcq distractor differs from the correct option in all parameter instances (checked).
