families.stem: For $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, the graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ has its highest point at $A(0^{\circ}, {=top})$ and its lowest point at $B(180^{\circ}, {=bot})$. Calculate the values of $a$ (the amplitude of the graph) and $q$ (the vertical shift of the graph). Write your answer as $a=\ldots$ and $q=\ldots$.
solution: The highest point of the graph is $A(0^{\circ}, {=top})$ and the lowest point is $B(180^{\circ}, {=bot})$, so the graph runs from $y={=bot}$ up to $y={=top}$.
The distance from the bottom of the graph to the top is ${=top}-{=paren(bot)}={=top - bot}$. This distance is twice the amplitude, so $a=\frac{{=top - bot}}{2}={=a}$.
To find $q$, compare with an unshifted cosine graph of the same amplitude, $y=a\cos\theta$ with $a={=a}$. Its highest point is at $(0^{\circ}, {=a})$, because $\cos 0^{\circ}=1$.
The highest point of our graph is at $(0^{\circ}, {=top})$, so the graph has been shifted up by ${=top}-{=a}={=q}$ units. So $q={=q}$.
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$. Check: at $\theta=0^{\circ}$, $a+q={=a}+{=q}={=top}$.
families.notes: Entry-point version of book ex6-6-3 (top point at 0 degrees, bottom point at 180 degrees). The book shows the curve in a figure; here the stem states which point is the highest and which the lowest, which is exactly what the figure tells the student, so the item stands without a diagram. All values are whole numbers, a > 0 and q >= a, so the whole graph sits on or above the x-axis (lowest value 0 to 5, highest at most 15). Answer is a = (top - bottom)/2 and q = top - a, the book's own method (half the top-to-bottom distance, then the shift of the point compared with the unshifted a cos theta). Unique answer: a + q = top and -a + q = bottom. The book's fractional case (a = 1/2) is deliberately not sampled so the key never depends on fraction rendering in a values marker.

families.stem: For $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, the graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ passes through the point $A(90^{\circ}, {=q})$ and has its lowest point at $B(180^{\circ}, {=bot})$. Calculate the values of $a$ (the amplitude of the graph) and $q$ (the vertical shift of the graph). Write your answer as $a=\ldots$ and $q=\ldots$.
solution: For an unshifted cosine graph $y=a\cos\theta$, the point at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ has $y=0$, because $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$.
Point $A$ is at $(90^{\circ}, {=q})$, where an unshifted graph would have $y=0$. So the vertical shift is $q={=q}$.
The line $y={=q}$ is therefore the middle of the graph. The lowest point $B$ is at $y={=bot}$.
The distance from the middle of the graph to its bottom is the amplitude: $a={=q}-{=paren(bot)}={=a}$.
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.
families.notes: Generalises book ex6-8-33 (and ex6-6-4): the point at 90 degrees gives q because cos 90 degrees = 0, and the distance from that middle line to the lowest point at 180 degrees gives a. The book only prints q = 0; here q runs from -4 to 4 (0 included, which reproduces the book case). 'Lowest point at 180 degrees' fixes a > 0, so 'amplitude' is correct wording. The stem does not say that A lies on the middle line: the student is meant to see that from cos 90 degrees = 0, as the book's solution does. Whole numbers only; lowest value ranges from -9 to 3.

families.stem: For $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, the graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ has its y-intercept at $(0^{\circ}, {=bot})$ and its range is ${=bot}\le y\le{=top}$. Calculate the values of $a$ and $q$. Write your answer as $a=\ldots$ and $q=\ldots$.
solution: The range gives the lowest and highest values of the graph: $y={=bot}$ and $y={=top}$.
The graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ is centred on the line $y=q$, halfway between its lowest and highest values: ${=bot}+{=paren(top)}={=bot + top}$, so $q=\frac{{=bot + top}}{2}={=q}$.
At $\theta=0^{\circ}$ we have $\cos\theta=1$, so the y-intercept is $(0^{\circ}, a+q)$. The y-intercept is $(0^{\circ}, {=bot})$, so $a+q={=bot}$.
Substitute $q={=q}$: $a={=bot}-{=paren(q)}={=a}$.

Check: ${=h}$ is the distance from the middle line $y={=q}$ to each end of the range, so $|a|={=h}$. The value of $a$ is negative because the graph starts at its lowest value, so it is a reflected cosine graph.
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.
families.notes: Advanced because it uses the objective's own pair of facts, the y-intercept (0 degrees, a + q) and the range, and carries a twist the book's section on the effect of a uses: here a is always negative (the graph starts at its lowest value and is a reflected cosine). The value |a| is half the range, q is the midpoint of the range, and the y-intercept then fixes the sign: a = intercept - q. Unique answer for every instance. q is never 0 so the midpoint step is not trivial; whole numbers throughout (|a| 1 to 5, q -4 to 4, range endpoints within -9..9). The stem deliberately does not call a the 'amplitude' (amplitude is |a|). The sign is always negative on purpose, to keep every instance at the advanced level; a family with a random sign would hand half its instances back to the basic tier. Two blind-solver traps to expect: answering a = +h (missing the reflection) and q = the highest value.

families.stem: For $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, the graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ has its highest point at $(0^{\circ}, {=top})$ and its lowest point at $(180^{\circ}, {=bot})$. Which of the following is the equation of the graph?
solution: The highest point is $(0^{\circ}, {=top})$ and the lowest point is $(180^{\circ}, {=bot})$. The distance from the bottom of the graph to the top is ${=top}-{=paren(bot)}={=top - bot}$.
This distance is twice the amplitude, so $a=\frac{{=top - bot}}{2}={=a}$.
An unshifted graph $y={=a}\cos\theta$ has its highest point at $(0^{\circ}, {=a})$. Ours is at $(0^{\circ}, {=top})$, so the shift is $q={=top}-{=a}={=q}$.
The equation is $y={=a}\cos\theta+{=q}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the full height of the graph as a
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the whole distance from the lowest point to the highest point as the amplitude a, instead of half of it. The amplitude is measured from the middle line to the top (or bottom), not from the bottom to the top.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the highest y-value as the vertical shift q
proposed_misconceptions.description: Reads q straight off the y-value of the highest point (the y-intercept), forgetting that this value is a + q and already contains the amplitude.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Swaps a and q
proposed_misconceptions.description: Finds the right two numbers but puts the shift in front of cos and the amplitude at the end, confusing which of a and q stretches the graph and which moves it up or down.

families.notes: Multiple-choice form of the same skill, kept because the catalogue of misconceptions for this objective was empty and each distractor here is a specific, diagnosable slip (not halving; reading q off the top; swapping a and q). The three declared misconception ids are new proposals. Parameters are chosen so every option is a different equation and no coefficient is 1 (a 2..5, q 2..7, q != a, so the options never read '1cos'), and q is positive so every option has a plus sign. The stem differs in every instance (it carries the two points), so distinct_by_choices is not set. 20 distinct instances.

families.stem: The function $f(x) = {=a}\cos(x - {=p}^\circ) + {=q}$ can also be written in the form $f(x) = {=a}\sin(x + h^\circ) + {=q}$, where $-180 < h \le 180$. Find the value of $h$.
solution: Use the shift rule for the two graphs: $\cos\theta = \sin(\theta + 90^\circ)$, so the cosine graph is the sine graph shifted $90^\circ$ to the left.
Here the angle is $\theta = x - {=p}^\circ$, so $\cos(x - {=p}^\circ) = \sin(x - {=p}^\circ + 90^\circ)$. The amplitude ${=a}$ and the vertical shift ${=q}$ do not change.
Combine the two angles: $-{=p}^\circ + 90^\circ = {=h}^\circ$, so $f(x) = {=a}\sin(x + h^\circ) + {=q}$ with $h = {=h}$.
families.notes: No figure. The book's questions read two sine/cosine graphs from a diagram; this advanced family works on the stated objective sentence instead (cos θ = sin(θ + 90°)) and adds the twist that the angle is x - p rather than plain θ, so the learner must substitute into the book's identity and combine the shifts. Answer is h = 90 - p, checked numerically for all 12 values of p (p = 90 excluded because h would be 0); h ranges over -70..70, always inside the stated window -180 < h <= 180, so it is unique and no mod-360 ambiguity arises. Negative h (p > 90) is deliberate: it tests the sign of the shift. Only the book's own identity and its meaning as a horizontal shift are used; no reduction formulas or negative-angle identities.

families.stem: The graphs of $f(x) = {=a}\sin x + {=q}$ and $g(x) = {=a}\cos x + {=q}$ are drawn on the same set of axes for ${=lo}^\circ \le x \le {=hi}^\circ$. How many times do the two graphs intersect in this interval?
solution: The graphs meet where $f(x) = g(x)$, that is ${=a}\sin x + {=q} = {=a}\cos x + {=q}$. The amplitude and the vertical shift are the same for both graphs, so they cancel and the equation becomes $\sin x = \cos x$.

The sine and cosine graphs cross where they have the same value. In one period, $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, this happens at $x = 45^\circ$ and at $x = 225^\circ$. These crossings are $180^\circ$ apart and the pattern repeats every $360^\circ$, so there is a crossing at every $x = 45^\circ + 180^\circ k$ for whole numbers $k$.
In the interval ${=lo}^\circ \le x \le {=hi}^\circ$ the first crossing is at $x = {=first}^\circ$ and the last is at $x = {=last}^\circ$, a distance of ${=last - first}^\circ$ apart.
With one crossing every $180^\circ$ the number of crossings is $\frac{{=last - first}}{180} + 1 = {=n}$.
families.notes: No figure. The book's basic questions count intersections of two drawn sine/cosine curves on 0 to 360 degrees; this is the same question asked of the algebraic pair over a longer interval, so the learner must know where sine and cosine cross (45 and 225 degrees) and that the crossings repeat every 180 degrees. f and g share the same amplitude and vertical shift, so the intersection set is exactly the solutions of sin x = cos x, i.e. x = 45 + 180k, independent of a and q. All interval ends are multiples of 90 degrees, which are never crossings (those are odd multiples of 45), so no endpoint ambiguity. Answers over the 32 admissible intervals are 2, 3 or 4 (counts confirmed by brute-force sign-change scan). The solution uses the special-angle values sin 45 = cos 45 that Grade 10 already has; it does not introduce tan x = 1.

families.stem: On the same set of axes, the graph of $f(x) = {=a}\sin x + {=q}$ and the graph of $g(x) = {=a}\cos(x - {=p}^\circ) + {=q}$ are drawn. Which single horizontal shift of the graph of $f$ gives the graph of $g$?
solution: Use $\cos\theta = \sin(\theta + 90^\circ)$ with $\theta = x - {=p}^\circ$: $g(x) = {=a}\sin(x - {=p}^\circ + 90^\circ) + {=q} = {=a}\sin(x + {=s}^\circ) + {=q}$.
So $g(x) = f(x + {=s}^\circ)$. Replacing $x$ by $x + {=s}^\circ$ moves every point of the graph of $f$ ${=s}^\circ$ to the left.
The graph of $g$ is the graph of $f$ shifted ${=s}^\circ$ to the left.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Reverses the direction of the horizontal shift
proposed_misconceptions.description: Finds the right size of shift between the sine and cosine graphs but reads the sign the wrong way, so a leftward shift is reported as rightward (or the reverse).

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ignores that cosine is already a 90 degree shift of sine
proposed_misconceptions.description: Reads cos(x - p) as 'the graph of f shifted right by p', using the number inside the bracket as the whole shift and forgetting that the sine and cosine graphs are themselves 90 degrees apart.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Believes cosine is sine shifted 90 degrees to the right
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses cos(theta) = sin(theta - 90 degrees) instead of sin(theta + 90 degrees), so the 90 degrees is added to the other shift in the wrong direction.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Reads x - p as a shift to the left
proposed_misconceptions.description: Knows cosine is sine shifted 90 degrees to the left but takes the minus sign in (x - p) to mean a further leftward shift, so adds 90 and p instead of subtracting.

families.notes: No figure. Natural mcq: a choice of direction and size of one shift, and every distractor is one specific, diagnosable slip (direction reversed; forgets the 90 degree offset; wrong sign in the identity; minus read as left). The correct answer is 'left' for every instance because p is kept below 90 (p = 45 is excluded so the 'p right' and 's right' options are never the same text). families.stem: The graph of $g(\theta)={=a}\tan\theta$ is drawn for ${=L}^{\circ}\le\theta\le{=R}^{\circ}$. Which one of the following is the domain of $g$?
solution: A tangent graph has a vertical asymptote at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and another one every $180^{\circ}$ (its period), in both directions. The graph never reaches an asymptote, so those values of $\theta$ are not in the domain.
The factor ${=a}$ only stretches the graph vertically (and reflects it in the $\theta$-axis when it is negative). It does not move the asymptotes.
In the interval ${=L}^{\circ}\le\theta\le{=R}^{\circ}$ the asymptotes are at $\theta={=ea}^{\circ}$ and $\theta={=eb}^{\circ}$, which are $180^{\circ}$ apart.
Every other value of $\theta$ in the interval is allowed, including the two end values ${=L}^{\circ}$ and ${=R}^{\circ}$.
Domain: $\{\theta : {=L}^{\circ}\le\theta\le{=R}^{\circ}, \theta \ne {=ea}^{\circ}, {=eb}^{\circ}\}$

proposed_misconceptions.label: Thinks the tangent graph has no excluded values
proposed_misconceptions.description: Treats the tangent like the sine and cosine graphs, whose domain is the whole interval, and gives the whole interval as the domain without leaving out the asymptotes.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Puts the asymptotes where the graph crosses the axis
proposed_misconceptions.description: Takes the asymptotes to be at the x-intercepts (0 degrees, 180 degrees, 360 degrees ...) instead of at 90 degrees and 270 degrees, so leaves out the intercepts instead of the asymptotes.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Thinks the tangent graph repeats every 360 degrees
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the period of sine and cosine for the tangent graph, so gives a period of 360 degrees, or finds only one asymptote in a 360 degree interval instead of two.

families.notes: Models the book's only question for this objective (ex6-8-55a, domain of g(theta) = -tan theta on 0 to 360 degrees, answer {theta : 0 <= theta <= 360, theta not 90, 270}). The window is always 360 degrees long and starts at a multiple of 180 degrees, so there are always exactly two asymptotes and neither is an end value. The book's marker is a set-builder interval that cannot be typed and marked reliably, so the family is mcq; every distractor is one diagnosable error. The options use literal LaTeX braces \{ and \} for set-builder notation (not followed by '=' so they should pass through the template untouched): please check the rendered options once. a is never 0 and never +-1 so the stem never prints '1\tan' or '-1\tan'.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta)={=a}\tan\theta {=sq} {=qa}$ is drawn for ${=L}^{\circ}\le\theta\le{=R}^{\circ}$. Which one of the following correctly gives the period, the $y$-intercept and the asymptotes of the graph?
solution: Period: the tangent graph repeats every $180^{\circ}$. Here $a={=a}$ only stretches the graph vertically and $q={=q}$ only shifts it up or down, so the period stays $180^{\circ}$.
$y$-intercept: put $\theta=0^{\circ}$. Since $\tan 0^{\circ}=0$, we get $f(0^{\circ})=({=a})(0) {=sq} {=qa}={=q}$, so the $y$-intercept is $(0^{\circ}, {=q})$.

Asymptotes: a tangent graph has an asymptote at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and another one every $180^{\circ}$, in both directions. Shifting the graph up or down does not move them, so in this interval they are at $\theta={=ea}^{\circ}$ and $\theta={=eb}^{\circ}$.
The correct option is: period $180^{\circ}$; $y$-intercept $(0^{\circ}, {=q})$; asymptotes $\theta={=ea}^{\circ}$ and $\theta={=eb}^{\circ}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Thinks the tangent graph repeats every 360 degrees
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the period of sine and cosine for the tangent graph, so gives a period of 360 degrees, or finds only one asymptote in a 360 degree interval instead of two.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Thinks the tangent graph always passes through the origin
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives the y-intercept as (0, 0) because tan 0 = 0, forgetting that q shifts the whole graph so the y-intercept is (0, q).

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes tan 0 degrees to be 1
proposed_misconceptions.description: Substitutes tan 0 degrees = 1 into a tan(theta) + q and gives the y-intercept as (0, a + q) instead of (0, q).

proposed_misconceptions.label: Puts the asymptotes where the graph crosses the axis
proposed_misconceptions.description: Takes the asymptotes to be at the x-intercepts (0 degrees, 180 degrees, 360 degrees ...) instead of at 90 degrees and 270 degrees.

families.notes: Standard tier: reading the period, y-intercept and asymptotes off the equation y = a tan(theta) + q, which is the point of the objective once q is present (q moves the intercept but not the period or the asymptotes). Each distractor changes exactly one of the three statements and names one error. Window is 360 degrees long, starts at -180 or 0 so theta = 0 lies inside it and the y-intercept is on the drawn graph; two asymptotes, none at an end value. q is never 0 and a + q is never 0, so (0, q), (0, 0) and (0, a + q) are always three different options. The sign of q is printed through a string let ('+' / '-'). x-intercepts for q different from 0 are deliberately not asked: they need solving a tan(theta) + q = 0, which the book does not model for this objective.

families.stem: The graph of $f(\theta)={=a}\tan\theta {=sq} {=qa}$ is drawn for ${=L}^{\circ}\le\theta\le{=R}^{\circ}$. Which one of the following is the range of $f$?
solution: Next to each asymptote the tangent graph goes off to $+\infty$ on one side and to $-\infty$ on the other, so between two asymptotes it passes through every $y$-value. It has no highest or lowest point.

The factor $a={=a}$ stretches the graph vertically (and reflects it if it is negative) and $q={=q}$ shifts it up or down. Neither of these puts a limit on how high or how low the graph goes, so there is no amplitude as there is for sine and cosine.
No value is missed either: at $\theta={=m}^{\circ}$ we have $\tan {=m}^{\circ}=0$, so $f({=m}^{\circ})={=q}$ and the value $y={=q}$ is reached. The graph does not level off at $y={=q}$.
Range: all real numbers, $y\in\mathbb{R}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gives a tangent graph a bounded range using a as an amplitude
proposed_misconceptions.description: Treats a as an amplitude and q as the shift of the middle line, so gives the range q - |a| <= y <= q + |a| as for a sine or cosine graph.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Leaves y = q out of the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: Carries over the hyperbola idea that the shift q is a horizontal asymptote that is never reached, so gives y in R, y not equal to q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gives the range of sine and cosine
proposed_misconceptions.description: States -1 <= y <= 1 for the tangent graph, ignoring both that tangent is unbounded and the effect of a and q.

families.notes: Standard tier: the range characteristic of y = a tan(theta) + q. The correct answer is the same every time, so the variation is in a, q, the window and in the three distractors, which all depend on a and q. The window is 360 degrees long and starts at -180, 0 or 180 so it always holds a full branch between two asymptotes (range is all reals on it) and a multiple of 180 degrees where tan = 0 (used to show y = q is reached, ruling out the 'y not equal to q' option). q is never 0, so q - |a| and q + |a| can never reproduce the -1 to 1 option. The sign of q is printed through a string let.

params.why: the interval must contain at least one asymptote

families.stem: Consider $f(\theta)={=a}\tan\theta {=sq} {=qa}$ for ${=L}^{\circ}\le\theta\le{=R}^{\circ}$. For how many values of $\theta$ in this interval is $f(\theta)$ undefined?
solution: $f$ is undefined exactly where the graph has a vertical asymptote. A tangent graph has an asymptote at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and another one every $180^{\circ}$ (its period), in both directions: $\ldots, -270^{\circ}, -90^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}, 270^{\circ}, 450^{\circ}, 630^{\circ}, 810^{\circ}, \ldots$ The values $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$ do not move the asymptotes.
The first asymptote at or after ${=L}^{\circ}$ is at $\theta={=first}^{\circ}$.
The last asymptote at or before ${=R}^{\circ}$ is at $\theta={=last}^{\circ}$. An end value of the interval counts if it is an asymptote, because $f$ is not defined there.
From ${=first}^{\circ}$ to ${=last}^{\circ}$ is ${=d}^{\circ}$, which is ${=k}$ steps of $180^{\circ}$. There is one more asymptote than there are steps: ${=k}+1={=count}$.
So $f(\theta)$ is undefined for ${=count}$ values of $\theta$ in the interval.
families.notes: Advanced tier: the book's domain idea (the asymptotes are left out of the domain) pushed over intervals longer than one period, with the twist that an end of the closed interval may itself be an asymptote (L or R equal to -270, -90, 90, 270, ...) and must be counted. a and q are in the stem but do not matter (the point of the characteristic). The first and last asymptotes are found with modulo arithmetic shifted by +720 so no operand is ever negative; every instance has at least two asymptotes (first <= last is also enforced). Largest R is 900, largest count is 6 or less. The sign of q is printed through a string let; q is never 0.

records.notes: The book has a single question for this objective (ex6-8-55a, the domain of g(theta) = -tan(theta) on 0 to 360 degrees; figure viewed, with asymptotes at 90 and 270 degrees and x-intercepts at 0, 180 and 360 degrees). No misconceptions were catalogued, so eight new ids are proposed, and a shared id carries the same label in every family that uses it. All four families keep to the book's own characteristics of y = a tan(theta) + q: domain, range, period 180 degrees, y-intercept (0, q), and asymptotes at 90 degrees plus multiples of 180 degrees. They never ask for x-intercepts when q is not 0, because that needs solving a tan(theta) + q = 0, which the book does not model here. Four families are returned rather than three because range is a distinct skill with its own diagnosable errors, so there are two standard families. Three things to check in the engine: the mcq options use literal LaTeX braces \{ and \} for set-builder notation; the sign of q is built with the string literals '+' and '-' in a let; and the numeric family uses the % and // operators on non-negative integers only.

families.stem: A tangent curve has an equation of the form $y=a\tan\theta+q$. Point $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$ and point $B$ is at $\left(45^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$; both points lie on the curve. Determine the values of $a$ and $q$.
solution: The constant $q$ shifts the graph up or down. For an unshifted tangent graph, point $A$ would be at $\left(0^{\circ}, 0\right)$. Here $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$, so the graph has been shifted upwards by ${=q}$. Therefore $q={=q}$.
To find $a$, substitute $q={=q}$ and point $B$, $\left(45^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$, into the equation. Remember that $\tan 45^{\circ}=1$.
$\begin{aligned}y&=a\tan\theta+{=q}\\{=yb}&=a\tan45^{\circ}+{=q}\\{=yb}&=a(1)+{=q}\\{=yb}-{=q}&=a\\{=a}&=a\end{aligned}$
The complete equation is $y={=a}\tan\theta+{=q}$. Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the y-value of B as a
proposed_misconceptions.description: Reads a straight off the y-coordinate of point B (a = y_B) because tan 45 degrees is 1, forgetting that the graph is shifted by q, so a = y_B is given instead of a = y_B - q.

families.notes: Entry point of the skill: both a and q positive integers, second point at 45 degrees where tan = 1, so y_B = a + q. Models ex6-6-6 and the upward-shift half of ex6-6-5. The book's figure is not reproduced (the family format carries no image): both labelled points are given in words as coordinates, exactly as the book's stems state them. a starts at 2 so the stated equation never reads 1tan. a != q so the two values are never confusable in the answer.

families.stem: A tangent curve has an equation of the form $y=a\tan\theta+q$. Point $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$ and point $B$ is at $\left(45^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$; both points lie on the curve. Determine the values of $a$ and $q$.
solution: The constant $q$ shifts the graph up or down. For an unshifted tangent graph, point $A$ would be at $\left(0^{\circ}, 0\right)$. Here $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$, so the graph has been shifted downwards by ${=abs(q)}$. Therefore $q={=q}$.
To find $a$, substitute $q={=q}$ and point $B$, $\left(45^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$, into the equation. Remember that $\tan 45^{\circ}=1$.
$\begin{aligned}y&=a\tan\theta-{=abs(q)}\\{=yb}&=a\tan45^{\circ}-{=abs(q)}\\{=yb}&=a(1)-{=abs(q)}\\{=yb}+{=abs(q)}&=a\\{=a}&=a\end{aligned}$
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Loses the sign of q
proposed_misconceptions.description: Reads the y-intercept (0 degrees, -3) as q = 3, or after substituting q = -3 subtracts 3 from y_B instead of adding 3, so that a and/or q carries the wrong sign.

families.notes: The book's typical exercise with the graph shifted DOWN (q a negative integer), second point at 45 degrees; y_B = a + q can be negative, zero or positive. Models ex6-8-34. NOTE: the book's printed solution of ex6-8-34 writes a(-1) for a tan 45 degrees (its answer a = 1 is nevertheless right because of a second sign slip); this family's steps use tan 45 = 1 throughout and do not reproduce that line. Figure not reproduced; both points are given as coordinates in the stem. a may be 1: the solution therefore does not print the complete equation, so it never reads 1tan.

families.stem: A tangent curve has an equation of the form $y=a\tan\theta+q$. Point $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$ and point $B$ is at $\left(135^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$; both points lie on the curve. Determine the values of $a$ and $q$.
solution: Point $A$ is the $y$-intercept: at $\theta=0^{\circ}$ we have $\tan 0^{\circ}=0$, so $y=a(0)+q=q$. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is ${=q}$, therefore $q={=q}$.
To find $a$, substitute $q={=q}$ and point $B$, $\left(135^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$, into the equation. Using a calculator, $\tan 135^{\circ}=-1$, so the tangent is negative at point $B$.
$\begin{aligned}y&=a\tan\theta+q\\{=yb}&=a\tan135^{\circ}+\left({=q}\right)\\{=yb}&=a(-1)+\left({=q}\right)\\a&=\left({=q}\right)-\left({=yb}\right)\\&={=a}\end{aligned}$
Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Uses tan 135 degrees = 1
proposed_misconceptions.description: Substitutes a point at 135 degrees using tan 135 degrees = 1 (the value of tan 45 degrees), so a = y_B - q is found instead of a = q - y_B and a comes out with the wrong sign.

families.notes: Advanced: fractional coordinates (the book's own twist in ex6-6-5, here halves) and the second point read at 135 degrees, where tan is -1, so y_B = q - a and the second point lies on the other branch of the curve. 135 degrees is a labelled value on the book's own theta-axis (0 to 180); the method is unchanged (q from the y-intercept, substitute B, solve for a), but note for the reviewer that the book's three exercises all place B at 45 degrees, so the 135 degree point is the one step beyond them. q is a half-integer (k odd), a is a whole number from 2 to 6, so a and y_B can never be whole numbers by accident and a is unique. The marker answer is written with numerator()/denominator() holes so no LaTeX fraction reaches the plain answer. Figure not reproduced; both points are given as coordinates in the stem.

records.notes: Three families, one per tier (basic, standard, advanced). The listed gaps (basic, advanced) are both filled; a standard family was added because no family existed at any tier and the three book questions are the only standard material. No figure is reproduced: the family format carries no image, so each stem states the two labelled points as coordinates, as the book's own stems do. All three share the book's method: q is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept A (0 degrees, q), then point B is substituted into y = a tan(theta) + q to solve for a. Basic uses positive integers at 45 degrees, standard uses a negative integer q at 45 degrees (the downward shift of ex6-8-34, whose printed solution has a sign slip that is not copied), and advanced uses half-integer q and a second point at 135 degrees where tan is -1. The objective's misconception catalogue was empty, so three new ids are proposed (a-is-yb, q-sign-slip, tan135-positive), one per family; none is used on a distractor because all three families are expression/values, not mcq. All answers are marked as a "values" marker [a, q] with variables a and q. Instance counts: basic 25 distinct stems, standard 30, advanced 50.

families.stem: The graphs of $y=\frac{{=u}}{{=v}}x$ and $y=\frac{{=k}}{x}$ intersect at two points: $A$ in the first quadrant and $B$ in the third quadrant. Calculate the length of $AB$ in units.
solution: At a point where the graphs meet, the two expressions for $y$ are equal: $\frac{{=u}}{{=v}}x=\frac{{=k}}{x}$.
Multiply both sides by ${=v}x$: ${=u}x^{2}={=k*v}$. So $x^{2}={=xa**2}$ and $x=\pm{=xa}$.
Substitute into $y=\frac{{=u}}{{=v}}x$: $x={=xa}$ gives $y={=ya}$ and $x=-{=xa}$ gives $y=-{=ya}$. So $A({=xa}, {=ya})$ and $B(-{=xa}, -{=ya})$.
Let $D$ be the point on the $x$-axis directly below $A$. Then $OD={=xa}$ and $AD={=ya}$, so by Pythagoras $OA^{2}={=xa}^{2}+{=ya}^{2}={=xa**2+ya**2}$ and $OA={=d}$ units.
The line passes through the origin, so $O$ lies between $A$ and $B$, and by the same working $OB={=d}$ units. Therefore $AB=OA+OB={=d}+{=d}={=2*d}$ units.
families.notes: Model: book ex6-8-53c (y = x and y = 8/x, AB by Pythagoras through the origin). This family keeps the book's method but raises the demand: the line has a fractional gradient u/v, so the student must equate the two expressions themselves (the book hands over the points), solve x^2 = k*v/u, find both y-values, and add OA and OB. The gradient and k are built from primitive Pythagorean triples (u, v, w) so that A = (v*s, u*s), B = (-v*s, -u*s), OA = s*w and AB = 2*s*w are whole numbers in every instance (12 distinct instances: 6 triples x 2 scales). The stem names the quadrants so A and B are unambiguous without a figure. A blind solver using the distance formula reaches the same number.

families.stem: The graphs of $f(x)={=b}^{x}+{=k}$ and $g(x)=-{=a}x^{2}+q$, where $q$ is a constant, cut the $y$-axis at the same point $A$. The point $B$ lies on $f$ and the point $C$ lies on $g$, and both have $x$-coordinate ${=n}$, so $BC$ is a vertical line segment. Calculate the length of $BC$ in units.
solution: $A$ also lies on $g$, and $g(0)=q$. So $q={=q}$ and $g(x)=-{=a}x^{2}+{=q}$.
$B$ is above $C$ (${=yb}>{=yc}$) and $BC$ is vertical, so $BC=y_B-y_C={=yb}-({=yc})={=bc}$ units.
families.notes: Model: book ex6-8-50b (f(x) = 4^x and g(x) = -4x^2 + q, BC found by substituting x = 1 into both). In the book A(0, 1) is handed over; here the constant q is not given and f carries a vertical shift k, so the student must first let x = 0 to find the shared y-intercept (1 + k), deduce q, and only then evaluate both curves at x = n and subtract (several more steps than the book's standard question; the shift k cancels in the final length, which is deliberate). Wrong answers typically come from reading b^0 as b or as 0 when finding A, the catalogued errors mc:g10m6s7-1-2:power-at-zero-read-as-base and mc:g10m6s7-1-2:power-vanishes-at-zero. Parameters keep b^n <= 27 and n >= 1 so B is always above C and every answer is a whole number at most 62 (120 distinct instances). a starts at 2 so the coefficient is always printed.

params.why: the vertical shift is written with a plus sign, so it must be positive

families.stem: The graphs of $f(x)={=a}\cdot {=b}^{x}+{=k}$ and $g(x)={=m}x-{=c}$ are drawn on the same set of axes. $P$ is the $y$-intercept of $f$ and $Q$ is the $x$-intercept of $g$. Calculate the length of $PQ$ in units.
solution: For the $y$-intercept of $f$, let $x=0$: $f(0)={=a}\cdot {=b}^{0}+{=k}={=a}\cdot 1+{=k}={=yp}$. So $P(0, {=yp})$.
For the $x$-intercept of $g$, let $y=0$: ${=m}x-{=c}=0$, so $x={=xq}$ and $Q({=xq}, 0)$.

$O$, $P$ and $Q$ form a right-angled triangle with the right angle at the origin, where $OP={=yp}$ and $OQ={=xq}$. By Pythagoras, $PQ^{2}=OQ^{2}+OP^{2}={=xq}^{2}+{=yp}^{2}={=xq**2}+{=yp**2}={=xq**2+yp**2}$.
Therefore $PQ={=dist}$ units.
families.notes: Model: book ex6-7-3c (the y-intercept of 2^x + 1 is found by letting x = 0, with b^0 = 1) and the book's habit of turning intercepts into lengths (ex6-8-48b, 48c). The advanced step is the chain: y-intercept of an exponential with a coefficient a (so the intercept is a + k, not 1 + k), x-intercept of a straight line by letting y = 0, then the distance between the two intercepts by Pythagoras. The intercepts (xq, yp) are always the two legs of a Pythagorean triple so PQ is whole (152 distinct instances). Typical wrong answers come from reading b^0 as b or as 0, i.e. the catalogued mc:g10m6s7-1-2:power-at-zero-read-as-base and mc:g10m6s7-1-2:power-vanishes-at-zero. The base b does not change the answer, which is the point of the catalogued errors. a >= 2 so the coefficient is always printed, m >= 2 so the gradient is always printed.

records.notes: Only the advanced tier was missing, so I wrote three advanced families with different skeletons. Together they cover both halves of the objective: equating two expressions (hyperbola-line), and letting x=0 or y=0 and measuring (shared-intercept, intercept-span). I did not read the engine's source, so I stayed with plain interpolation and signs written in the template. No negative-coefficient formatting functions are used (signed, linear, quadratic or paren); parameter ranges keep every coefficient positive. I checked the arithmetic of every instance of all three families (12, 120 and 152 distinct parameter sets) with an independent script: whole-number answers, the b^n <= 27 and k >= 1 requirements, and the Pythagorean-triple construction. All three are numeric, so none carries a distractor or a misconception id. The three catalogued misconceptions apply to the wrong answers in shared-intercept and intercept-span, and the notes name them for the reviewer. I did not build a parabola-pair or line-parabola family: the distance between intersection points is irrational for integer gradients, and a horizontal-distance-only version would have been padding. The figure-based book questions (counting intersections on a trig graph, 46b and 47b) cannot be turned into diagram-free families, so no basic-tier work was attempted (and none was requested).

families.stem: Determine the range of $y = {=a}\operatorname{{=fn}}\theta {=signed(q)}$. Write your answer in the form $m \le y \le M$.
solution: The sine and the cosine of any angle lie between $-1$ and $1$: $-1 \le \operatorname{{=fn}}\theta \le 1$.
Multiply every part by ${=a}$. Because ${=a}$ is positive, the inequality signs stay the same: $-{=a} \le {=a}\operatorname{{=fn}}\theta \le {=a}$.
Now add the constant ${=q}$ to every part. The lowest value of $y$ is ${=q} - {=a} = {=lo}$ and the highest value of $y$ is ${=q} + {=a} = {=hi}$.
So the range of $y = {=a}\operatorname{{=fn}}\theta {=signed(q)}$ is ${=lo} \le y \le {=hi}$.
families.notes: Standard tier: the book's own exercise (ex6-7-3a/b, 2 sin(theta)+1 and 2 cos(theta)-4) answered by writing the range rather than picking it. a is a whole number from 2 to 6 (never 1, so the coefficient always prints), q is a non-zero whole number from -6 to 6, and the function is sine or cosine at random. Range is q-a <= y <= q+a. The book's printed options write the range with theta where y is meant (a typo in the book); this family uses y throughout. The marker is the closed interval [q-a, q+a]; the stem asks for the book's inequality form m <= y <= M. The two closed-end flags are written as 1, 1 (true) so that they parse in any plain-maths reader. The function name is rendered with \operatorname{...} so one template serves sine and cosine. Instances are distinct through a, q and the function (about 120).

families.stem: Which of the following is the range of $y = {=a}\operatorname{{=fn}}\theta {=signed(q)}$?
solution: The sine and the cosine of any angle lie between $-1$ and $1$: $-1 \le \operatorname{{=fn}}\theta \le 1$.
Multiply every part by ${=a}$. A negative multiplier reverses the inequality signs, and the ends $-1$ and $1$ become ${=c}$ and $-{=c}$, so $-{=c} \le {=a}\operatorname{{=fn}}\theta \le {=c}$.
Now add the constant ${=q}$ to every part. The lowest value of $y$ is ${=q} - {=c} = {=lo}$ and the highest value of $y$ is ${=q} + {=c} = {=hi}$.

So the range is ${=lo} \le y \le {=hi}$. The negative sign of $a$ changes which value of $\operatorname{{=fn}}\theta$ gives the lowest $y$, but the range is still ${=c}$ below and ${=c}$ above ${=q}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Lets the negative sign of a flip q as well
proposed_misconceptions.description: For an equation such as $y=-3\sin\theta+2$ the student reads the minus sign as applying to the whole right-hand side, so finds the range of $-(3\sin\theta+2)$ instead. The range is mirrored about 0 and the sign of $q$ is reversed, giving $-q-|a|\le y\le -q+|a|$.

families.notes: Advanced tier: the twist the book's method uses for a < 0 (the range is q+a <= y <= q-a, i.e. q-|a| <= y <= q+|a|). a = -c with c from 2 to 6; q is a non-zero whole number with |q| < 2c, |q| <= 6 and q != c, which guarantees that all five options are different and each is a proper interval (lower end below upper end) for both values of the option switch w. Distractors: ignores q (-c to c); q added at one end only (w picks which end: -c to q+c, or q-c to c); the sine/cosine-from-0-to-1 error carried over to a negative a (a times [0,1] plus q gives q-c to q, so the range ends at q instead of starting there; same catalogued id); and the new negative-sign-flips-q error (range of -(c sin + q)). mc:...:ends-are-the-equation-numbers is not used here (only four distractors are needed). Option texts carry $...$ as the stem does. The stem holds a, q and the function, so instances differ without distinct_by_choices. About 90 distinct instances. As in the standard family, the book's printed options say theta where y is meant; this family says y.

records.notes: Both listed gaps (standard, advanced) are filled; no basic family was written because the book's two MCQs already cover that tier. Standard is free response with positive a, written as an interval marker. Advanced is a negative-a MCQ with four named distractors, three from the catalogue and one new id (negative-sign-flips-q). Assumptions that I could not verify without the engine and that the reviewer should check: (1) interval(lo, hi, 1, 1) parses with 1/1 as the closed-end flags; (2) signed(q) renders a signed constant after the trigonometric term; (3) string literals such as ['sin', 'cos'][t] are allowed in a let param; (4) the app wraps option text in $...$ like any other text. The slugs interval-range and reflected-range differ in their first six letters (interv, reflec).
